maintopic: ONTARIO WINTER WHEAT-REMOVAL OF PRICE CEILING AS OF JUNE 18

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: ONTARIO WINTER WHEAT-REMOVAL OF PRICE CEILING AS OF JUNE 18
speechtext:
I have been asked by several hon. members to state the policy of the government with regard to Ontario winter wheat.
In considering Ontario winter wheat policy for the crop year commencing July 1. 1948, the government has decided that the price ceiling
on Ontario winter wheat can be removed and this action will be effective as of today, June 18. The present treasury payment of eight cents per bushel is discontinued with the removal of the price ceiling. This means that the price of Ontario winter wheat will be free to find its own level under prevailing conditions.
I am unable at the moment to state whether export control will be necessary or not in the case of Ontario winter wheat. If an international wheat agreement becomes operative on August 1, 1948, the export of Ontario winter wheat or Ontario winter wheat flour will be included under all the terms of such an agreement, and export control will be necessary in this case. The government hopes that this issue will be clarified prior to the harvesting of the 1918 winter wheat crop.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Salaries Act so as to provide an increase in the salary of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward1 Island from $7,000 to $8,000.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Perhaps I
should say a word on this resolution. As hon. members know, the salaries of lieutenant governors are fixed by the parliament of Canada. They vary in different provinces. For some time past the annual salary of the lieutenant governor in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec has been fixed at $10,000, and in six
other provinces at $9,000. The salary of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island has been $7,000.
During recent years, as hon. members know, the expense of maintaining government houses has risen considerably, and after reviewing the situation carefully the government felt that the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island, while he had not as many duties as some of the other lieutenant governors, had nevertheless to meet increasing obligations which he has not heretofore been called upon to discharge.
I would mention particularly that the lieutenant governors pay income tax on their salaries. In some of the provinces, government houses are provided by the province. That is the case in Prince Edward Island. That is also true in three or four other provinces. Where government houses are not provided, the provinces make other arrangements in the form of providing official quarters, allowances for expenditures and the like.
I understand that in Prince Edward Island the lieutenant governor has himself had to meet practically all the expenses of the maintenance of government house and secretarial expenses. While that is so, his obligations have increased materially during the last few years. In reviewing the whole situation, the government felt that parliament should be asked to grant an increase of $1,000 in the salary of the lieutenant governor of that province.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister indicate when the last adjustment was made in the salaries of lieutenant governors?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: I understand there has been no adjustment for forty years.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
May I be permitted to
make a few remarks with reference to this resolution? I was pleased indeed when I noticed that this resolution was to be brought before the house, but I was disappointed in the consolation increase of S1,000 being provided; because, as the Prime Minister has already stated, in six of the other provinces the lieutenant governors receive $9,000, and in the two larger provinces the salary is $10,000. When we compare these salaries with those paid to judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, the salaries of the lieutenant governors are really on a very low scale, in view of the duties and responsibilities pertaining to the office.
With reference to the salary of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island, I suggest that if it is based on the cost of living, his salary is out of proportion to the
Salaries Act

others, because the cost of living in Prince Edward Island is just as high as it is in any of the other provinces, including Ontario and Quebec. What is the price of butter today in Prince Edward Island, as compared with other provinces? The prices of cars and many other commodities are much higher. When we look at the position the lieutenant governor occupies as the representative of the king in the province, we wonder why the salary should be on such a low basis. In addition to the executive work the lieutenant governor of our province is called upon to do, he is the salesman- of the province to visitors who come from other provinces and countries.
I should like to see the resolution changed so that it would increase the salaries of all lieutenant governors; and at this time we should make the salary of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island equal to the salaries of those in other provinces.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
I am glad to support what has been said by the hon. member for Queens. Actually lieutenant governors are like the united nations, in that there are small and big ones-small powers and big powers. So long as there is a lieutenant governor in that province he is representative of His Majesty the King, and I cannot see why there should be any differentiation in the matter of salaries. Many visitors go to Prince Edward Island, and I suggest respect-full}'' to the Prime Minister that if he decides there should be an increase in salary it should be uniform for all lieutenant governors.
Most of these men are gentlemen of means -and rightly so, because the ordinary man could not fulfil the functions of the office. I do not see why we should be so stingy with lieutenant governors in any of the provinces. They should be on the same footing as representatives of the king, carrying the same honours and the same salaries and wearing the same uniforms.

It does seem strange to me, however, that it has been so easy during this session to have so many of these salaries increased to meet the increased cost of living and increased obligations of public officials, as contrasted with the difficulty we have in getting increases in pension benefits, veterans' allowances, superannuation for retired civil servants, old age pensions and family allowances to meet the same increased cost of living and the same increased obligations of Canadian citizens generally.
Almost every bill that we have put through this session

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND

Almost every bill we have put through this session has had in it a provision for raising salaries from $6,000 to $8,000, from $10,000 to $12,000, or from $12,000 to $15,000. It seems to me if the government admits that Canadians in these upper brackets are hit by the increased cost of living and by increased obligations, it should also recognize that the same is true right across the board. Either there should be an increase for the groups of people I have mentioned, or a serious and aggressive attempt should be made by the government to bring down the cost of living.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I am permitted I should like to qualify what I have said. I have suggested that the salary of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island should be raised to the same level as that of the lieutenant governors of other provinces. speechtext: At the present time it would appear that the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island receives 87,000. I do not know the gentleman, nor do I know who he is.

speechtext: If he is a Prince Edward Islander he is a good man.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
I have no doubt about that. I see, however, that there is considerable discrepancy in the salaries of these lieutenant governors. Those of Ontario and Quebec receive 810,000, while those of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta receive $9,000 each. Under this measure the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island would receive $8,000.
If the program of austerity is imposed on the lieutenant governors as well as on all other Canadians, they would probably curtail their receptions and save money thereby. To start a new trend in austerity, why not reduce the salaries of the lieutenant governors in all provinces to $7,000, so that their salaries would be equalized? Then they would be on a par with Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
I had not planned on entering this debate, but I had not read the measure before. It seems that the Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia receives only $9,000, while those of Ontario and Quebec receive $10,000 from the coffers of the people of Canada-and this at a time when my people are under water. There is not a chance in the world of my agreeing to that. The Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia five days ago was out with his good lady going through the water to help flood victims. And he should be underpaid? Nonsense! I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that we can raise the salaries of members of parliament, including myself, of the board of transport commissioners, and of everybody else in the higher brackets, but we have to fight to get increases in war veterans allowances and veterans pensions.
If there is to be any increase, then I believe with the hon. member for Temiscouata that all lieutenant governors should be paid the same, or those in the higher brackets should be reduced to conform with those in the lower; and if it is possible to move an amendment to that effect, with these Ontario members, I shall be delighted to move it.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not often that I have anything to say in this house, but this is one time I am going to say a few words. While I have no objection 5849-345
to increasing the salary of the gentleman mentioned, because it would seem an increase is justified in order to meet conditions as we find them today, I must comment upon the increases that have been made in the salaries of those in the upper brackets during the past few months, increases of $1,000, $2,000 and $3,000. Those salaries must be paid out of the receipts from income tax and so on. I cannot sit here and take it when I see that the poor man is receiving no alleviation this year from the burden of income tax. I will fight with every drop of blood I have to see that some alleviation is provided for the poor man by way of reduction in taxes so that he can at least make a living.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: When I listen to the hon. member for Springfield I wonder if we are not looking at this thing in the wrong way. Under our democratic system we have a governor general and lieutenant governors. The latter are paid salaries of $9,000 or $10,000 a year, but I believe we are getting $25,000 worth of services.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: Everyone knows that a man must have considerable wealth to be able to accept one of these positions. The lieutenant governors are willing to carry out these duties which we feel are necessary under our British system, and they sacrifice from $10,000 to $15,000 a year to keep up that tradition in a manner befitting representatives of the crown. I feel that we are getting a tremendous bargain, as it were, when these gentlemen are willing to act in this capacity.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARY OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: I just want to say one more word. I think what has been said by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni about the right of these people to carry on the tradition of their position applies equally to the ordinary Canadian. I have heard some persons speak who are aspirants for the position of lieutenant governor of Ontario some
Excise Act

time in the future. We have an excellent lieutenant governor in British Columbia who is spending from $25,000 to $50,000 of his own money every year. We had great difficulty in getting a citizen of sufficient means who was capable of handling the position. The members of the government know that.
In spite of what has been said by some who have aspirations to fill the position of lieutenant governor in the future, why should one be paid any more than the other? I have the greatest admiration for every one of these people and what they stand for, and I think they should all be paid the same.
(Mr. SHAW: I agree with the principle of ' this bill. I do not think increasing the salary of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island by $1,000 will make any difference as far as the treatment of Canadians in other categories is concerned. speechtext: Mr. ROBERT H. WINTERS (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendment made by the senate to Bill No. 300, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ACT OF 1934-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ACT OF 1934-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the definition of "sailing ship" in the act as it was received in this chamber from the senate was "any ship propelled wholly by sails." That meant that all ships equipped with auxiliary engines and sails came under the act for steamship inspection and for certification of officers. Maritime and west coast members thought that would result in hardship to our fishing fleets, which by and large are still of the sail type although they are all equipped with auxiliary engines. We therefore sought an amendment of the definition, and the minister was good enough to bring in a new definition, as follows:
"Sailing ship", except for the purposes of the load lines rules, means a ship propelled wholly by sails, and a ship solely employed in fishing not exceeding one hundred and fifty tons, gross tonnage, provided with masts, sails and rigging sufficient to allow her to make voyages under sail alone, and that in addition, is fitted with meehanical means of propulsion other than a steam engine.
The senate considered the wording of the amendment too stringent, with particular respect to the words "Sailing ship is a ship solely employed in fishing not exceeding one hundred and fifty tons, gross tonnage." The limiting phrase "solely employed in fishing" means that fishermen such as, for instance, the Lunenburg salt fishermen, who in the wintertime run their salt fish to the West Indies and other coastal ports, and other fishing vessels employed part-time in the coastal trade, would be obliged to submit to

Diplomatic Service Superannuation Act
steamship inspection and certification. The senate therefore struck out the words "solely employed in fishing not exceeding one hundred and fifty tons," and substituted "principally employed in fishing not exceeding two hundred tons," raising the tonnage to two hundred, because there are certain schooners engaged in the trade which are slightly over one hundred and fifty tons gross tonnage. That leaves the spirit of the amendment the same, making it applicable to the same type of vessels but to slightly larger vessels. The amendment in that form, Mr. Speaker, is acceptable to the government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ACT OF 1934-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is the final wording of the amendment? We have had the explanation, but the bill has not been distributed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ACT OF 1934-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from the explanation just given by the parliamentary assistant it would seem to me that the hon. gentlemen in the other place in making this change were solely concerned with the east coast codfishing schooners. When the bill was before the house the provision was that as long as a ship could make a voyage under sail it was to be exempt from steamship inspection regulations. Our ships on the Pacific coast have greater power and are really more seaworthy than those on the east coast, and the senate amendment differentiates between the two types of vessels used on the east coast and on the west coast. I find it rather funny. These so-called diplomats remind me of comic opera, of the Student Prince, with their uniforms and all that stuff. They should have small uniforms because Canada is a small country and therefore we should not have them too big, and they cannot work on stilts.
The other day the Ottawa Citizen had a very good article about the promotion of a high commissioner to ambassadorial rank. The conclusion of the editorial was how could the king raise the standard of men who are representing him to himself. It is a fine and subtle distinction on the divisibility of the crown. A Canadian ambassador would be the ambassador of the king of Canada, to the king of England, who is the same person. The ambassador is the representative of the head of the state to the head of another state. If the high commissioner of Canada to England were promoted to be ambassador he would be the representative of the head of the state of Canada, His Majesty George VI, to the head of the state of the United Kingdom, the same man, His Majesty George VI, but to a different crown in each case.
Of course, these men want promotion. It may be well deserved. It would raise their standard. It would raise them in importance and they would walk immediately after the royal family instead of walking after the dukes and barons, and all others, in important processions. Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member's speech may be very amusing, but this is merely a bill to correct three errors that I must confess we made last year. When the bill was brought before the house last year it did not provide for the rule that if one retires at a time when he is not entitled to any pension he can get his contributions back. That is now the rule which has been put into all the superannuation acts, and this bill proposes to include it here.
Another provision is to correct another error which I must admit. We provided that those who would want to have past service counted should have their contributions based, either upon the actual salaries they received, or the salaries they got when they were first appointed to external affairs. We found in two instances it gave the appointees the right to make contributions on less than the actual salaries they had been receiving, and we do not think that is proper. Therefore we are just taking out that and making it a requirement that their contributions will be based upon the actual salaries that will serve as a basis for determining the pension they will get.
The third point is this. Hon. members felt last year that this was going to be a very generous pension scheme. There are two or three of the thirteen who were appointed who have other military pensions, which means that they would get no benefits out of this. Therefore the third provision is that anyone who is appointed to External Affairs need not make the contributions if he will renounce any benefits from the act. These are the only three things that are provided.
The hon. member has said that some gentlemen appointed to diplomatic rank did not deserve any reward, and he mentioned two.
I can assure the hon. gentleman that they were not appointed with the idea of giving them any reward. It was after considerable pressure had been put upon him that Mr. Greene consented to become our high commissioner in Australia and warned us at the time that he did not expect to be able to serve there for more than a couple of years. He is one of those who would be entitled to take advantage of this bill. Since this bill was passed the only appointee who was not taken from the civil service was Mr. Turcotte, who was appointed consul general in Chicago.
The hon. member for Temiscouata says that consuls general should be under the Department of Trade and Commerce and not under the Department of External Affairs. That is a view as to which some good arguments might be advanced. But I can assure the hon. member that the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Trade and Commerce co-operate closely and that exchanges of personnel have been made. We have appointed to diplomatic rank, gentlemen who have served efficiently as trade commissioners. The trade commissioners are still under the Department of Trade and Commerce, but the consuls provide excellent service to the Department of External Affairs.
The hon. gentleman mentioned Mr. Scully in New York. The offices of Mr. Scully in New York would have had to be duplicated for the service of our delegation to the united nations if we had not had those facilities there. Elsewhere so far we have limited consular service. The consuls of course assist in the promotion of trade, but they also render assistance to Canadian nationals who happen to be abroad. In some places we require to have representatives of the Department of External Affairs who can come to the assistance of Canadian nationals who happen to need assistance. This house places at our disposal each year a revolving fund out of which we frequently have to make advances, which are returned, to Canadian nationals who happen to get into difficulties abroad.
The suggestion that there should be a division and that the consular service should be under the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce is one that is worthy of consideration, but no solution could be arrived at on this bill. Hon. members of the house will remember that formerly if a civil servant were dismissed, he did not get back his con-

Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer to a speech made by the hon. member for Lethbridge on June 8, as reported at page 4903 of Hansard, on a motion to go into supply, in which he made certain charges
and asked specific questions relating to two cases which have been brought to my attention.
I think the reply would come more properly under this item, which covers general administration, than any other. I regret that I and other members of the parliamentary committee were not in the house when the hon. member made his speech. The committee was in session on veterans affairs and was busy at the time. Neither did I have knowledge that the hon. member intended to discuss these matters. I did not know that he was interested in the two cases to which he referred. If I had known that, I would have been very glad to give him correct and complete information regarding them.
It will be noted that the complaints made by the hon. member the other day were apparently based upon representations made to him by Captain Walter H. Kirchner, of British Columbia. The committee will remember that in times past a number of serious charges had been made by Captain Kirchner, whereupon my predecessor appointed a commission composed of Doctor McCann, Doctor Blair, Doctor McGarry, Mr. Probe and Mr. Winters, all members of this house.
Last fall this commission went to British Columbia and conducted a thorough investigation into all charges made. Both cases referred to the other day were looked into by the commission at that time. The commission submitted its report to the government shortly after I became minister, and on March 9 last I tabled that report in this house. Although the report has been available since March, the hon. member made such unwarranted statements the other day, at the same time demanding replies to his questions, that I feel I should place on record the actual facts regarding these two cases. I do so, Mr. Chairman, much as I deplore the naming of individual veterans in this house, unless it is absolutely essential. But since they were named with regard to the complaints, I can do no other than follow suit now.
No. 77732, Sholto B. McClellan: Mr. McClellan is a veteran of world war I who served from November, 1914, to May, 1918, part of his service being in France. On enlistment his age was thirty-nine years. Following discharge from service, entitlement was conceded for myalgia and pension was awarded in accordance with the extent of disability resulting from that condition. Disability was assessed at 15 per cent and pension went into payment accordingly. Early examination took place on four subsequent occasions, but there was
542S
Supply-Veterans Affairs

no indication of any increase in disability. In December, 1923, application was made for treatment in respect of haemorrhoids and the commission conceded entitlement for this condition, which improved with treatment, and there was no resultant disability. In 1926, following discharge from treatment, it was considered that there was increase in the disability resulting from arthritis and pension was increased accordingly to 30 per cent. Again, in 1928, following treatment, there was considered to be further disability and pension was increased to 50 per cent. In 1929 he applied for bronchitis, which the commission ruled to be a post-discharge condition. This claim was heard by the pension appeal court in March, 1931, and was disallowed, as bronchitis was ruled as not attributable to service. During subsequent years he has been examined on different occasions and the pension continued at 50 per cent, which was in accordance with the degree of pensionable disability.
In 1939 he was in receipt of war veterans allowance, which was discontinued in 1942 owing to his having secured employment. As a result of representations received on behalf of this pensioner a re-examination was ordered, and this took place in August, 1947. The x-ray of both knees, both shoulders, spine and pelvis showed moderate hypertrophic-arthritis, and reports indicate that examination showed joint movements as practically full range. There was no evidence of haemorrhoids at the time of this examination, and pension was continued at 50 per cent, which was again considered to be a very fair one for the degree of pensionable disability.
It should be pointed out that the pensioner by this time is seventy-two years of age. This pensioner appeared before the McCann commission in Vancouver in January of this year, and on February 18, 1948, forwarded a statement regarding his case to the members of that commission. The statement was forwarded for the consideration of the commission, and instructions were issued to the Vancouver office on March 22, 1948, to recall him for pension medical re-examination with particular regard to his complaint regarding the assessment of any disability resulting from haemorrhoids.
In a letter which is dated April 2, 1948, he refused to appear. To sum up the case, this veteran of world war I has been fully compensated at all times in accordance with the degree of pensionable disability found on medical re-examination. It must be remembered that he is now seventy-two years of age, and age alone is quite a factor in his present

condition. I might add that there would appear to be no reason why he should not now apply for war veterans allowance.
We come now to the second case, No. V-52017, Connorton, F. W. (R.C.N.V.R.). Mr. Connorton served from December 1942 until March 1946, his entire period of service being rendered in Canada. Following discharge a condition of spondylolisthesis, which I am told by the doctors is something approaching difficulty with the lower spine, was diagnosed. And this I might say is a constitutional developmental condition. The commission ruled it to be pre-enlistment in origin and aggravated to the extent of three-fifths during his service in Canada, which was in Canada only.
His last examination was in January of this year when, to quote his own words, he made the following complaint:
My back feels fair except if I bend over any length of time it becomes painful at the upper part of the fusion and tends to stiffen up.
_ As a result of reports and specialists' opinions on file and a very thorough examination, his entire disability was assessed at 30 per cent. He has entitlement to an aggravation of three-fifths of that amount, namely IS per cent, and pension is in payment accordingly. It is of interest to note that when he reported for examination on March 15 of this year he stated he was working.
Questions were asked by the hon. member for Lethbridge, as reported in Hansard for June 8, 1948, at page 4903, with reference to Frank W. Connorton. The first question was: Did this man's condition partly result from an appendix operation in June, 1943?
The answer is: The man's condition had no relation to the appendectomy performed in June 1943, while he was in the active forces.
The spinal anaesthetic given at this time, for which eight punctures were alleged to be given, was investigated, and competent medical opinion states that there is no relation between the incidents surrounding this operation and his subsequent back disability.
The second question: Did his tragic final condition partly result from his effort to do work for which surgical bungling had unfitted him?
The answer: Careful examination of the medical treatment shows that there was no "surgical bungling" of this case.
The third question: Did his condition result in any considerable measure from a spinal fusion operation on November 15, 1945, apparently unsuccessful, and subsequent mismanagement on the part of government officials in the army?

Supply-Veterans Affairs
The answer: While the Department of Veterans Affairs was not responsible for this man's treatment until March 18, 1946, a review of his treatment that is available on his army file does not disclose any mismanagement on the part of government officials in the army.
The fourth question: Was his misfortune partly the result of a second unsuccessful spinal fusion operation on or about September 18, 1946?
The answer: The unsuccessful spinal fusions done on November 15, 1945, while he was under the medical care of the armed services, and again on September 18, 1946, while he was under the medical care of the Department of Veterans Affairs, are not unusual happenings in the treatment of such cases. These attempted fusion operations did not increase his disability even if they did not completely do away with it.
The public inquiry held under P.C. 4980 to which reference was made earlier, included investigation of such cases in Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver. Connorton's case was one of those investigated. Some of the conclusions arrived at as a result of investigation are contained in the report of January 8, 1948, paragraph 9 of which states:
The commission is satisfied with, and finds no basis for complaint concerning the organization, operation and facilities of Shaughnessy hospital and the other institutions inspected.
The commission is satisfied with, and finds no basis for complaint concerning the qualifications of departmental doctors. In two cases veterans harboured resentment against the psychiatric service. Some lack of experience on the part of a junior psychiatrist and the inability of these patients to understand the reasons for psychiatric methods-although allegedly the reasons were fully explained to them -were factors which led to this resentment. The commission is satisfied however that this did not detract from the professional value of the psychiatrist's work nor from the adequacy of the treatment. On the whole, the commission is fully satisfied with the high degree of competence of all departmental doctors.
The commission found that the medical and surgical treatments and the results attained are quite satisfactory and of a high calibre-as high as in any hospital in Canada. The percentage of successful operations at Shaughnessy hospital is, in the opinion of the commission, well in line with that obtaining anywhere in the profession.
The commission examined fully the cases of low back pains and resulting disability because of the emphasis placed by Mr. Kirchner on this group. The commission concluded:
It was established to the satisfaction of the commission, after detailed questioning of professional witnesses, that while the operation is not alw-ays completely successful, the percentage of successes at Shaughnessy is at least as high as
that obtaining elsewhere. Back fusion is regarded as a major operation and is only undertaken at Shaughnessy hospital after a consultation at which it has been decided that the operation is in the veteran's best interests and is likely to lead to improvement of his condition. The commission wishes to comment particularly on the high qualifications and exceptional competence of the neurosurgeon specialists at Shaughnessy hospital.
I may say that the part of the report that I quoted was from a unanimous report of the commission.
It will be seen that the commission investigating the type of case of low back pain and investigating specifically the treatment afforded Connorton concluded that the very best of medical attention is afforded this group of cases in the Department of Veterans Affairs and that this treatment is not always successful, but the percentage of successes in the department is as high as in the best treatment institutions in the country.
Further direct questions were asked in the House of Commons on June 8, 1948, page 4906 of Hansard, second column. I believe it is the opinion of the best medical men in the dominion-the report would indicate that this is also the opinion of the commission set up under P.C. 4980-that the treatment services given to veterans by the Department of Veterans Affairs are of a very high quality. I do not feel that from a treatment standpoint there are injustices done in the case of Connorton, and I believe that he, and cases similar to his, have received and will receive the best of treatment without the alleged injustices.

I wish to assure the minister that we do not want to hold up the veterans affairs estimates, but I should like to make a suggestion. The final report of the veterans affairs committee has not been made to the house, and possibly will not be made for several days. I think it would be better if the first item was held over until the report is received. We could pass the other items that could be passed and in that way make headway. After the final report of the committee has been received and we have had some time to study it, we can then deal with the first item, possibly in a short time.
I agree with that.

I know it is a comfort to the committee to have the minister give this report on these two men. The committee will have noticed, however, that the complaint made by Mr. McClellan was in the words which I read into Hansard, as reported on page 4903, as follows:
What we are complaining about is that our records have been mishandled, or, in real truth.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

falsified, to make it look as if we were not entitled to pensions.
My evidence clearly shows that the charges are true.
The committee was entitled to expect that the minister would adduce evidence in the McClellan case to show that there was no foundation for his complaint, namely, that there had been falsification of the records as far as McClellan was concerned. The minister has said nothing about this serious aspect of the matter and I submit that the committee is entitled to a thorough treatment of that phase of dealing with veterans. I will leave the McClellan case for the time being.
I return now to the Connorton case. The committee will have noticed that in dealing with the Connorton case the real challenge of the material which I placed on Hansard was not met. I think it would be well for me to give a moment or two to that matter. The report presented by the minister is accurate, it is moderately worded, but it does not meet *the challenge. I stated that this young man Connorton was well and strong when he joined the forces.
In order to aid the minister in going still further into this question, which I am sure the committee will want him to do, I should like to ask four questions. First, was Connorton formerly an apprentice machinist who for two years prior to enlistment had been serving with the Vancouver Engineering Works Limited? Second, as such was he engaged daily in heavy lifting work and classified by that company as being well above the average of the employees engaged in that class of heavy lifting work? Third, was he classified by the manager of the Vancouver Engineering Works as a first-class workman, intelligent, cheerful and co-operative, and also as one who had demonstrated that he possessed the qualities of a first-class machinist? Fourth, was he classified by the director of apprenticeship of the province of British Columbia as one who would be a valuable asset to the armed forces at his trade occupation?
If the answers to those questions should prove to be "yes", and if it should be established that there is unchallengeable documentary evidence to prove that the answers should be "yes," then the problem which will confront the minister's department will be to show the committee and the country how it came about that a boy who was eighteen years of age on enlistment and who possessed those qualifications should be turned out of the service in 1946 an almost complete wreck as far as doing the kind of work that he had done before was concerned, and yet was ruled as being the victim of a pre-enlistment disability.

That is the question. We can use technicalities and doctors' terms and all that sort of thing, but the simple fact remains that that boy of eighteen years of age went into the service in apparently perfect physical condition, at least as far as practical considerations were concerned, and he left the service a wreck and yet is reported as suffering from a pre-enlistment disability.
This young man was discharged broken in mind and body. I shall not ask questions on that aspect of the case at present, but would point out that according to the man's own testimony he was suffering on discharge from a prostate gland; he had a bad leg, with muscles tired and locking and the leg aching all the time; he had lost the use of the toes of his left foot after the first spinal fusion; he could not even stand the work of oiling on the Princess Elaine. Oiling is a kind of work that does not require heavy lifting. He also says that after his operation for spinal fusion on November 15, 1945, he wore a body cast and a leg cast until approximately the .middle of March, 1946. After that he wore a Taylor brace until June, 1946, and he never again was able to do anything like the heavy work which he had been able to do
The minister said in his statement that the boy was working on March 2, 1948-the minister will correct me if I have not the exact date-but he does not tell us what the boy was working at. I will wager that the boy was not able to do the heavy machine work that he was doing at the age of eighteen before he enlisted, and I make this general observation: that in view of the amount of money he is receiving he would simply have to work or starve. The minister's statement was vague and general.
The next question I asked was: Did this man's condition result partly from an appendix operation in June 1943? In order to enable the minister to go into this matter more thoroughly may I ask him to prepare and give to the committee at a later date answers to the following questions:
1.	Did Connorton undergo an appendix operation in the service in June, 1943?
2.	Was he given a local anaesthetic for the operation?
3.	Was the anaesthetic administered by a departmental medical intern?
4.	Was a needle inserted in Connorton's spine eight times before the anaesthetic was effective?
5.	Did the man suffer excruciating pain in this anaesthetic operation?

Supply-Veterans Affairs
6. Did the medical intern instruct the nursing sister and an orderly to "pin the man down"?
7.	Was the man fourteen days in bed after this appendix operation?
8.	Did he complain of his back being sore ail that time, and did the departmental doctors inform him he would experience back trouble for about two months, when the condition would "clear up"?
By the way, it is rather unusual after an appendix operation to wait two months before the condition clears up.
9.	Did they say this was the usual experience of men receiving spinal anaesthetics to localize an operation?
10.	Was he given pills to relieve the pain in his back?
11.	Was the man bothered with prostate trouble after this operation, and was he given sulphanilamide drugs, penicillin and electrotherapy treatment for this condition?
12.	Does the man claim that prostate trouble is still with him?

Would the hon. member permit an interruption? I do not question his sincerity in asking the twelve questions, but he will appreciate that the questions he asks refer to an operation conducted in 1943 while the man was within the armed services and under their medical care. The questions relate, I take it, to conversations in the operating room and afterwards. I can assure the committee that it will be impossible for my department, and I doubt whether it will be possible for the defence department, to answer all these questions at this time. I have tried to give the hon. member, as briefly as possible, such information as I have at this time on both cases, and I shall attempt to give him any further information I have. Now that he has put the matter forward, I think that should cover the situation fairly adequately.
While I am on my feet I might refer to one statement he made as to the falsification of documents; I presume he meant army documents. Any evidence there may have been on that question was looked into by the McCann commission, and nothing has been brought to my attention, in the report or otherwise, that would lead me to believe that there was falsification.

I am glad that the minister has made that statement, because according to the terms of reference of the McCann commission and the press release which was made from Ottawa concerning its activities, I gather that the commission was not appointed to examine the question of the
falsification of the records. The press release dated December 6, 1947, concludes with these words:
The terms of reference call for investigation of adequacy of treatment in D.V.A. hospitals, qualifications and competence of D.V.A. doctors, and the adequacy of pension considerations.
May I submit to the minister-and I do this in all kindliness, not with any desire to criticize him or his department but simply to get at the facts-that the McCann commission was appointed apparently to investigate charges which had been preferred by the member for Acadia and the member for Swift Current in 1947, and those charges had nothing in the world to do with the efficiency of the doctors in the department; so that when the McCann commission by its terms of reference was given the task of investigating the efficiency of the doctors, that was something that was utterly beside the main point at issue which everybody supposed the commission was appointed to investigate.
I shall have a good deal more to say about this matter as the days go by. From what I have been able to gather concerning the McCann commission, the reasons for its appointment, and the way it did its work, as well as the terms of reference to the commission, I have a suspicion that quite a lot of explaining is necessary on the part of a good many people in the department before this house can be satisfied with the McCann commission.
The next question I raised was:
Did Connorton's tragic final condition partly result from his effort to do work for which surgical bungling had unfitted him?
I should like to ask the minister some questions which he might submit to his department on this question. But before I do that may I refer to one thing that he said in his reply a moment ago? He said that all such matters as are called for in the questions which are asked under the last question would have to do with conversations which would take place in hospital and elsewhere. That is true; but the important thing is that Frank W. Connorton has submitted a deposition in which he solemnly declares the facts as called for in each of these questions. Unless the department can show that Frank W. Connorton was falsifying in his deposition it will have to accept Connorton's words as being valid. That would be my general opinion on the matter.
Now for the questions in respect of my ' second question:
1.	After hospitalization, did Connorton join the minesweeper Outard as stoker, November, 1943?
Supply-Veterans Affairs

2.	Did he complain that his back was then still bothering him?
3.	Did he complain that his left leg also began to bother him when doing heavy lifting, the muscles becoming tired and locked?
4.	Does he complain that his leg condition is still with him?
5.	Was he given a one-man board by Doctor Whitelaw in July, 1944, and X-rayed, and subsequently classed as A-l physically fit?
6.	Did he subsequently complain to another departmental doctor, a Doctor Prior, that his spine was still bothering him?
7.	Did Doctor Prior state that he would charge him with "malingering" if he complained again?
8.	Was he also examined by other departmental doctors at the 'Givenchy barracks, Victoria, British Columbia, and did they say there was nothing wrong with him?
Probably the minister will have to say that he has not the information in his department with which to answer these questions, but they are vital. If they suggest the truth, and I am sure they do, then they suggest some pretty serious charges against the men who had to deal with this splendid young man.
The next question I asked was this:
Did Connorton's condition result in any considerable measure from a spinal fusion operation on November 15, 1945, apparently unsuccessful, and subsequent mismanagement on the part of government officials in the army?
I should like to ask several questions to help the minister get the facts concerning that matter for the committee. They are as follows:
1.	Was Connorton examined by Doctor Ross Robertson, neurosurgeon, Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver, British Columbia, and did that physician allege the man had an immature spine?
This is the first of a series of questions. May I just stop here to point out that if the answer to that question is found to be. yes, then everyone in this house and in the country can see that there has been culpable blundering on the part of the medical men who had to deal with this soldier before Doctor Ross Robertson came to him. I continue with my questions:
2.	Did Doctor Ross Robertson tell the man he would need as remedial treatment a spinal fusion operation to knit the spine?
May I pause here-

speechtext:
Order. The hon. member for Wentworth suggested a short time ago that the item should stand, and that the hon. member who is asking the questions be given an opportunity to forward his questions to the minister. I wonder whether it

would save time if the hon. member would consent to sending his questions to the minister so that he could properly answer them when the committee meets again. If the hon. member would do that, we would save a lot of time.
I can understand the desirability of sending these questions and having a private answer given so that the country as a whole would not know about these questions.
That is not it at all.

I should like to point out that I have the floor. I want to fight this thing out with the hon. member who just rose and interfered. If this young man can be found to have been the victim of a miscarriage of justice through the various agencies which this parliament has appointed to give such young men justice, then there is only one place where hon. members can weigh that matter, and that is before the high court of parliament. Therefore these questions have to be asked and answered in public so that the people themselves can determine the justice of the treatment of this young man. All I am doing in speaking at this time is taking up the case of this young man. I should like to ask the hon. member who rose a moment ago how he would feel if this man were his son.

On a point of privilege, I should like to answer the hon. member who has just spoken. I want him to understand that I am just as much interested in all these cases as he is. I merely rose to correct a false impression on his part. There has been no suggestion in this chamber this morning that the questions should be privately answered. The chairman suggested that the hon. member could send his questions to the minister, who could answer them later, publicly, in another meeting of this committee. That is all I said when I rose. I want the hon. member to understand distinctly that I am just as much interested in these cases as he is, and always have been.
I apologize to the hon. member immediately and unreservedly.

I appreciate that. I am endeavouring to do only what I conceive to be my duty in the circumstances.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Before the committee took recess for lunch, I was asking several questions bearing upon the question I asked on June 8: Did the condition of Connorton result in any considerable measure from a spinal fusion operation on November 15, 1945, apparently unsuccessful, and subsequent mismanagement on the part of government officials in the army? I asked two questions. May I ask several more:
3.	Was Connorton given a spinal fusion operation on November 15, 1945?
4.	Did the man lose the use of his toes in the left leg as a result of this operation?
5.	Has subsequent remedial treatment for the toes proved ineffective?
6.	Was he subsequently examined in the Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver, British Columbia by the neurosurgeons, Doctors Boucher, Naden, Starr, Thompson and Black?
7.	Did these neurosurgeons turn him over to Doctor Stanley, departmental psychiatrist, and did Stanley state that there was nothing wrong with the man except in his imagination?
8.	Was the man then discharged from the Shaughnessy hospital without pension for his condition, and did he accept employment as a fireman in the engine room of the CT.R. steamer Princess Elaine?
9.	Was he compelled to give up this employment after two weeks on account of his back giving out?
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that when those questions are answered, the answers will have an important bearing on the question whether or not this young man's ills are the result of military service. I asked one more question on June 8. It was this:
Was his misfortune partly the result of a second unsuccessful spinal fusion operation on or about September 18, 1946?
I have three questions to ask that will help the minister in his investigations pertaining to that question. They are as follows:
1.	Was Connorton again admitted to Shaughnessy hospital on September 18, 1946, and subsequently given an exploratory operation by opening up the spine?
2.	Was he in consequence given a second spinal fusion operation? If so, when?
3.	Has the man stated he cannot face the operating table again because of the suffering he has undergone during those two operations and because his powers of resistance are now undermined?
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that when the minister finishes answering those questions, in so far as the information will enable him to answer them, he will be ready to agree with
me-and I believe I am only one of the total membership of this committee who has this opinion-that this man is certainly suffering as a result of military service and not as a result of a pre-enlistment disability.
I should like to ask the minister one or two more questions which do not bear particularly on the questions I raised on June 8. The first one of these has to do with Connorton.
I should like to ask the minister to conduot a careful examination into the whole situation which is involved in this question and then report to the committee all the details of evidence and considerations upon which the Canadian pension commission, after studying the case of Frank W. Connorton, concluded "that this-the condition of prespondylolisthesis-is of pre-enlistment origin", as stated in paragraph 1 of their decision of May 10, 1947, dated at Ottawa.
Then I wish to ask a question on the case of another man who was under review by the McCann commission, whose case somewhat resembles the Connorton case. I refer to Stanley L. Walsh, V-86097. In this case, after considerable correspondence had taken place, Brigadier J. L. Melville wrote a lettei to Walter H. Kirchner, dated September _2, 1947, in which he used the following words in paragraph 2:
. . the condition under review is partly due to a constitutional defect and under the circumstances must be considered as of pre-enlistment origin . . .
I should like to have all the details of the evidence and considerations upon which the Canadian pension commission arrived at that decision concerning Stanley L. Walsh. ^
There is another matter which I desire to mention at the present time. On June 8 I had some rather harsh things to say concerning psychiatrists. I wish to ask several questions on the matter of psychiatrists and to have the minister get the answers and inform the committee and the house in detail with respect to these gentlemen. The questions are as follows:
1.	Has a psychiatrist in such a position as,
say psychiatrist to Shaughnessy hospital, power to destroy utterly a veteran's chance for pension by simply reporting "this man is definitely neurotic"?	_
2.	Can a key psychiatrist free the commission from the responsibility of furnishing either the applicant or his representative with a summary of evidence?
3.	Does this arrangement give the psychiatrists a stranglehold upon the medical profession?
4 (a). In order for the psychiatrist to exercise over the veteran such fearful power as is

Supply-Veterans Affairs
indicated in questions 2 and 3, is it necessary merely for the psychiatrist to label the veteran a "psychotic"?
(b). If a psychiatrist labels a man as having "emotional instability", will that fact also deprive the man of pension rights?
5.	Do psychiatrists use what is called the pentothal test?
6.	What is the nature of this test?
7.	Do psychiatrists use what is called the truth serum test?
8.	Is there any difference between the pentothal and the truth serum test?
9.	If so, what?
10.	Does the patient under the truth serum test go into a sort of trance, a state somewhat resembling hypnosis?
11.	While the patient is in that state, can the psychiatrist make the patient answer questions according to the way they are framed, thereby causing the patient to say almost anything he, the psychiatrist, may desire the patient to say?
12.	Can the answers of the patient obtained in such a trance be used to defraud the veteran patient of his rights to pension and proper treatment?
13.	Was this very technique employed against certain Hong Kong veterans so to deprive them? For instance, were Hong Kong men who survived the terrible tortures and privations of Japanese prison camps told in their examinations that they were not suffering from those most harrowing experiences but that they were suppressing childhood fantasies and fears?
14.	Did Doctor J. P. S. Cathcart, while in office as a sort of official psychiatrist for the Department of Veterans Affairs, publish the following statement?
Popular belief to the contrary, mental diseases are not common hazards of war even for men in the field. If a man is mentally sound on entering the army, navy or air force he runs no greater risk of having his faculties upset than if he continued in civilian life.
Did he declare the belief that wartime service brings mental upset is unfounded and arises from ignorance fostered by ill-advised propaganda?
15.	Did the Department of Veterans Affairs for a time base the treatment of veterans policy upon the principle laid down in that pronouncement, namely, that psychosis or neurosis was automatically a pre-enlistment disability?
16.	If so, for how long a period and between what dates was this principle used as the basis for departmental treatment of veterans?
17.	If not, when and by what pronouncement was the principle and the policy announced in Cathcart's statement changed?

18.	How many veterans' cases were disposed of by the department on the basis of pre-enlistment neurotic or psychotic disability during the period throughout which the Cathcart principle was in use by the department?
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid 'that when these questions are all accurately answered, and members of this house are able to draw their conclusions as to what sort of treatment our veterans have received at the hands of psychiatrists, there will be something like a sensation in the house and throughout the country.
I have just this general comment to make before leaving this aspect of my questioning of the minister. First, the evidence I have indicates too strongly that psychiatrists attached to the Canadian veterans affairs department are employed occasionally to deprive a deserving veteran of the financial reimbursement to which he is legally entitled. Second, certain of these psychiatrists are of the type exemplified by General Brock Chisholm, a man who gave the definite impression that he was distinctly materialistic, if not crude, sordid or even sadistic in his outlook upon human life. And, third, such so-called psychiatrists, men who should be called rather pseudopsychiatrists, are not to be named in the same breath with those noble psychiatric healers who in Britain, the United States, Australia and other lands are, with Christlike devotion to spiritual values, salvaging wounded souls stricken by the desecrating hand of war.
When I spoke on June 8 I made remarks which had general application to psychiatrists throughout the country who were employed by the veterans department. I know that the true psychiatrists, the men who are genuine healers, can be a blessing to the mentally stricken, and these men wherever they are in Canada will readily pardon me for any reflection upon them which may have been implied, because they will have readily recognized that some of the things which have been done by so-called psychiatrists in this country have brought into disrepute the whole class of psychiatrists. They will recognize immediately also that it is time something was done to rid the country of the pseudo-psychiatrists who apparently are employed by the veterans affairs department as agents to deprive men of their rights rather than to heal them of their mental ills.

Mr. Chairman, during the session it has been my opportunity since January to provide members of the house with a chance to consult with my officers on any individual cases regarding whom complaints have been laid, by themselves or by somebody in their constituency or somebody they knew.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I would have been very happy if the hon. member for Lethbridge had brought these cases to my attention at any time. I do not complain of the fact that he has brought individual cases before this committee, nor do I mind the work entailed by the large number of questions he has placed on the record this afternoon. I will assure him now in the first place that many of these questions are of the kind that a member of parliament would like to ask of my officials across a desk, or to ask me if I could give the answer orally. If it is his desire to sit in with any of my officials, who are quite familiar with all these cases, I shall be glad to furnish that opportunity.
I would point out that many of the questions are based of course on the service period of the veteran. As the committee knows, we inherit the documents pertaining to that service. We have no authority to go back into army service and seek witnesses who happened to serve at that time, but we will undertake, if he wishes, to make that information available to him personally, and, if that is not satisfactory, then to the best of our ability we will attempt to answer questions appropriate to my department and submit them to the committee.
Having made that statement, and in conformity with the request of the hon. member for Wentworth, I am prepared to permit this item to stand for the time being, especially in view of the fact that the final report of the veterans affairs committee has not been submitted. Before doing so, however, I shall make an explanatory statement regarding item 532.
This vote in 1948-49 provides $633,480 for expenditures of the war service records division which in previous fiscal years were provided for through the Department of National Defence. If it were not for the responsibility for the operation of the war service records division by the Department of Veterans Affairs, the moneys provided in this vote for the year 1948-49 would show a decrease as compared with 1947-48. I wish just to make that explanation. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, we might take up the next item, No. 533.
Item stands.
533. District administration, $3,805,120.

There is a district office at 55 York street, Toronto, where tens of thousands of cases are handled. I understand that instead of making it necessary to write to Ottawa the district principle is to be applied, so that if anyone has a complaint regarding a pension or some other payment-and after the meetings of the pension committee in the last several years, there are many kinds of extra allowances and other payments-that
person could get speedy adjustment of his claim at district offices. Is my understanding in that respect the correct one?
I see hundreds of people coming out of that building at closing time. Many of these cases come to my attention, particularly in the summer months when some of the other members may be away. Has the district officer and his staff in the building at 55 York street, next to the Royal York hotel, power to deal with a case, or must such case be referred to Ottawa before a decision can be given? It is pointed out in some cases that the regulations are not broad enough to permit the district office to act. This condition may have been changed since the meeting of the committee last session.
If it is necessary to get in touch with Ottawa it would cause a great deal of delay. Some of the soldiers and their families have no houses. That is one of their complaints, among others.

I am glad the hon. member has brought this point to my attention, because it has been the aim of the deputy minister to do just what he has suggested, namely, in so far as possible to obtain decentralization of authority. Only last Friday I had the pleasure of visiting all the offices in the Toronto region and discussing with the administrator and the members of his staff the very point my hon. friend has mentioned.
I am assured that at the present time there are very few bottlenecks.

Would the minister also consider the matter of telephone service in Toronto government offices? To my mind the telephone service is all wrong, because one cannot find the right number in the telephone book. What I say applies to every department of the public service in the Toronto district. One goes to one building only to find that the office has been moved to some other building. Surely a large business such as one finds at 55 York street, one which runs into an expenditure of many millions of dollars in pensions and allowances, should have a modern telephone system such as would be found in Eaton's or Simpson's stores. Sometimes I have had to spend half a day walking from one building to another before I reached the right spot. Finally I am directed to go to 465 Bay street, where the hon. member for Peel used to have his law office.
And you, too.

A good deal of time is wasted travelling around because one cannot find the correct telephone number. An office for soldiers has now been opened in the city hall, where complaints can also be made.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

Sometimes I am asked, "How can one find the number, or find the new office, because the number in the telephone book is not the correct one?"
This causes a serious inconvenience. The office at 55 York street serves several counties. Some of these soldiers and their families come to the city on Saturdays and find that the offices are closed. I am not complaining about offices closing on Saturday-far from it; but surely a skeleton staff could be left which could take complaints and thereby save the necessity of these people returning on another day. They cannot afford to make these trips; furthermore, the trains are congested. I believe if the minister would consider my suggestion much time might be saved. In Toronto these departments are moving every day, and the result is that the telephone numbers are not correct. We do not know where to find the different departments. Will the minister consider making the necessary change?

I believe I can understand how this may have happened. It has been our attempt so far as possible to concentrate all the activities in the Toronto region under one roof. The Veterans' Land Act administration was moved to that building within the last month or two. I can understand how in some instances the new location might not match up with that given in the telephone directory. I can assure the hon. member this condition will be taken care of.
As to the matter of availability on Saturdays, let me say that our offices are kept open until one o'clock Saturday afternoon, in Toronto and elsewhere.

I want to tell the minister that, up to now, I am satisfied. I consider his appointment a great improvement in the Department of Veterans Affairs. I shall not add further praise, because too much praise sometimes brings trouble.
I have only one question to ask. A friend of mine had a son in the army. The son died. He was a father, and the grandfather has taken charge of the children. In virtue of the legislation about to be passed, will there be some increase in the pension payable to the grandchildren?
If the veteran father was a pensioner over 50 per cent, the children would be in receipt of pension as orphans.
How much more will they receive? [DOT]
Their new pension will be increased by 25 per cent.

There is a certain matter about which I have spoken to the minister on several occasions since his appointment. He has promised to look into it, and I believe he has now done so. Today I am asking him to review the situation so that we may know exactly where his department stands in the matter. I refer to the abandoned hospital at Kirkfield Park in the constituency of Portage la Prairie, outside of Winnipeg.
If my figures are correct, and if my memory serves me aright, when the project was started the government spent about a quarter of a million dollars, perhaps more, in construction. At the present time all one sees is some substantial foundations and rough buildings. Two or three weeks ago the minister and his parliamentary assistant looked over the situation. I have not yet received a report, although I have spoken to the minister on several occasions and one other hon. member has discussed the matter in the house several times. Either the original plan to construct this hospital was a mistake, or the abandonment of the hospital was a mistake. That has never been made clear in this house.
It seems to me that if the government do not intend to proceed with the construction and use of these buildings, some effort should be made to find somebody willing to make use of what has been constructed. In view of the large expenditure of money I think the committee is entitled to an explanation from the minister. Was it a mistake to plan to construct this hospital? Was it a mistake to abandon construction? What is intended to be done with these buildings and foundations which are lying there as a not very pleasant reminder of a large expenditure of money and the use of scarce building materials?

During a recent visit to Winnipeg with my officials I visited the site of the Kirkfield Park health and occupational centre, as it was intended to be. In October 1945 the wartime committee on hospitalization approved this project, which would have comprised 200 beds at an estimated cost of $700,000. At that time there was a scarcity of hospital beds in Winnipeg and patients were crowded at the Deer Lodge hospital. Moreover, the type of treatment which would have been afforded in this centre would have been of inestimable value for wounded veterans under convalescent treatment here and those coming back from overseas.
My hon. friend has asked whether it was sound reasoning to decide to construct this hospital. He knows more about the circumstances than I do. It was the opinion of those who were responsible then that it was sound

Supply-[DOT]Veterans Affairs
to go forward to provide this accommodation quickly as a health and occupational centre. If it could have been completed at the time it was expected to be finished, it would have served a most useful and important function in the treatment of wounded veterans. That was in 1945. However, factors have arisen which were not predictable at the time which makes the completion of this accommodation at the present time quite doubtful.
Added accommodation was obtained at Brandon military hospital to relieve the congestion at Deer Lodge. Then there were unforeseen delays in construction, and the project was discontinued in July, 1947. At that time relatively little progress had been made. Some $313,000 had been expended, and the completion of the original idea would have called for the expenditure of approximately S600,000 more.
I think it will answer my hon. friend's question if I say that in the opinion of my department it is not considered sound to recommend the completion of the hospital along the lines of the original idea. Perhaps it would answer his last question if I told him that we are actively exploring the possibility of these buildings being used, either by other federal departments or by other public bodies. I found it necessary to write the present minister after he came into office-and in passing I wrant to congratulate him upon how well he is taking care of his department. In my letter to the minister of February 2. 1948, I said:
Personally, I cannot understand this at all. Here is a man now beyond sixty-five years of age who, in his youth and strong young manhood, offered himself in defence of the empire for service in South Africa. The long marches in that hot climate, so hot in the daytime and so cold at night, undermined his health. During all his life, he has not had the physical strength that he should have had, and now, late in life he finds it necessary to make application for war veterans allowance or pension.
The reason for not granting Mr. W. a pension seems to be that his wife owns a property. I

Supply-Veterans Affairs
know the property well. It is a duplex. Well, everyone knows that duplexes are next to impossible to sell.
If they were compelled to sell I doubt whether they would get $5,000 for it.
The report sent in about the income of the family gives the income much higher than it really is. Apparently the Toronto office has sent down an erroneous statement on the income of that family. I know it is small. I know the family well. At the present time this noted soldier is in a serious condition. Last Saturday, as I walked down my home city street, I saw him being lifted out of a motor car and carried into his home. I said, "Why, are you not improving?" He said, "I have been in the hospital. They wanted to take off my leg. I cannot stand on the leg, it is in such a state." Surely there is something wrong somewhere.
Here is a man who was in the full strength of his youth. He went into the South African campaign, which everyone who was there knows was not the best kind of campaign for anybody, especially for the health of those who came from a northern climate such as ours. He came back, and all his lifetime he has suffered from disabilities incurred in that campaign. But he never applied for a pension at anyr time. His record was good. He marched and fought all the way from Cape Town to where the war ended at Bloemfontein or Pretoria. To me it is a shocking shame that he who is penniless himself, who has not a farthing, has to ask his wife for a car ticket if he wants to go downtown. This country never intended that anything like that should happen. He is not asking for the full amount of the war veterans allowance. He would be satisfied with half the amount, because his wife has a very small income. It is so small that I would not call it an income at all. It would not compare for a moment with the ordinary person's income. She and her home can hardly exist on it. That is the state in which he finds himself.
Last year the previous minister said that this man was entitled to the war veterans allowance. What happened after that? Who told the minister that he was not entitled to the allowance? The present minister has been very good. I am one of those who like to support him. I ask him to take this case into consideration and give this noted soldier a square deal. He has not had it. No soldier has a square deal who is treated as this man has been treated. Parliament does not want any soldier to be treated in that way.
This man is penniless. Why should he have to ask his wife for a car ticket? He cannot work. The minister has a copy of the affidavit
on file. I will send him another copy of it. His doctors, and the others who have been associated with him, say that he must not do anything because his heart is bad. I said a moment ago that when I saw him he had to be carried out of the car into his home. If that is not a disability I do not know what a disability is.
I will leave the case with the minister. I am not going to ask him to refer to it at the moment. I have urged the case as strongly as I can. I have known this veteran for twenty-five years. I know that he has not earned anything, because he has not been able to work. He has been only an encumbrance to his wife. Why should he not have the war veterans allowance for himself personally?

I assure my hon. friend that I shall be only too glad to look into the case. I would not want to make a statement on it now, but I shall see that it is looked into, particularly in the light of the amendments that have been passed by the house this year, to see if by any chance that should change the situation.

are directed to go to an immigration office or tc somebody else. In weather such as we shall have in the next three months it is pretty difficult to bring little children with them. Some of these young people come from the west and the east. Some are just looking for work, and they get into some minor trouble. They are just sent down, and their parents are not even notified. Money is being spent at 55 York street, and efficient work is being done there. A large number of them are first offenders. In my opinion, a legal officer should be provided who could proceed to the police court in the morning to assist these young people. Some of the Christian churches have a representative in the police court. The time has come when something should be done. Some of these people cannot pay a fine. I tried to get the law of England, the Summary Offenders Act, brought in here to give them time to pay, both soldiers and civilians. In Britain they have thus closed half the prisons. When I look at the reports of the provincial and federal prisons, the Attorney General of Canada's institutions, I find that few of these young people are getting in there. Where lack of money was the prime cause of their withdrawal.

It is most unfortunate that their whole original investment should be lost, as it can be lost in these cases.

legal offices for training only and for no other purpose, there is no question about continuation, but there are some complications which we are ironing out and I am sure we shall be able to straighten them out satisfactorily.

Has the department given consideration to an increase in the allowances paid to university students?
