What is the departmental policy with regard to the hospitalization of veterans for ailments other than their war disabilities? I think we should have that picture cleared up. Apparently this is a new departure, although I believe that for many years a veteran without resources could get hospitalization without any allowances. This charging a veteran the same rate that would be charged in a civilian hospital is something comparatively new, and I believe the minister should give us the whole story.
While he is doing that, will he also say whether consideration has been given to providing hospitalization for war widows? Apparently Australia decided this year to provide free hospitalization for war widows and their children in government hospitals. I have a press dispatch from Brisbane, dated March 1 of this year and reading as follows:
Australia Gives War Widows Hospital Care
Australia's 2il,000 war widows and their 13,000 children under 16 years of age will shortly get free medical treatment at war veterans' hospitals.
Under a new scheme they will get specialist care, a full range of medicines and drugs, and X-ray diagnosis.
At present widows and children receive only limited medical care from the government.
What is the policy of the Canadian government with regard to war widows and their children?
May I deal with the second point first? Up to date we have no authority under our statutes for taking care of war widows or their children.
Has any consideration been given to adopting a policy of that kind?
It was discussed this year in the veterans affairs committee and representations were made there. However, nothing has been done.
Is the government considering the question quite apart from the veterans affairs committee?

Yes, we have considered it. I should like to refresh my mind as to 'the details of the hospital policy in connection with those who are not pensioners, and I will submit full details to the committee later on.
It would be most beneficial if the minister could give us the full picture of what, is being done.
It has not changed greatly, but I shall do that.

Two weeks ago I asked the department if a veteran who had been ordered by the proper authorities to report to a military hospital for treatment would be entitled to transportation to and from his home, including taxi cabs if necessary. May I ask that question again?
The answer is yes.

What would 'the minister think if the following were proved to be the fact? A veteran went to Christie Street hospital and received treatment. After his 'treatment was completed, he was told by the nurse to get ready to leave on a certain date, that a taxi cab would be there to transport him to the union station at a certain hour. The veteran got ready and he asked for his transportation and was told that it was not ready for him. Fortunately his son had called at- the hospital for him and he paid for the taxi cab. He inquired from the taxi cab driver who had been ordered by the authorities at Christie Street to pick up this veteran whether he had paid, and the taxi eab driver immediately replied that no such arrangements had been made.
This veteran was completely disabled, but fortunately he had his son with him and he paid for the taxi cab. It took several weeks of correspondence finally to obtain the transportation from the institution. I say in all friendliness to the minister that I hope he will make immediate inquiry about the actions of the men and women in that hospital who are supposed to provide transportation for disabled veterans.
Transportation should be sent to these men before they leave their homes. We cannot surmise that they will all be men able to pay for their own transportation. They may be living on a small allowance. Certainly, when they leave the institutions they should be treated in the same way as we were during the last war. When we left the hospital a pass was placed in our hands and they said, "Good-bye and good luck to you." But here a man is sent to the station in a taxi which has been ordered by someone in authority at Christie Street, and when he arrives at the station he finds that no arrangements had been made for his rail or taxi transportation. It may be discovered that some person is doing something that should not be done, something not according to the rules in the book. If a veteran arrives at a hospital and, not knowing the rules, does not ask for transportation, it should automatically be given to him; or if upon discharge he does not ask for trans-
Supply-Veterans Affairs

portation he should be followed up with a letter saying, "You were entitled to your transportation and we forgot to give it to you when you left the hospital. Here it is." I am sure that if the minister will make an investigation at Christie Street hospital he will iind that every disabled veteran has not been provided with transportation.
If the hon. member will give me the details of this or similar cases I shall be glad to look into them.
I shall be glad to do that.

I want to take the minister into another phase of hospitalization which I think is important, and to present it properly I shall have to go back into history. I refer to the domiciliary care of veterans on a small pension or receiving the war veterans allowance who are now hospitalized in such places as the Red Chevron in Toronto. If their pension is not sufficient to provide them with certain necessary amenities they are granted $5 a month for comforts and $5 a month for clothes. This policy resulted from the deliberations of the committee of 1922 and was implemented in 1924. Between then and 1936 the amount was raised to $20 a month; I presume $10 a month was for comforts and $10 a month for clothes. But in 1936 the *department reduced the amount to $10 a month-$5 for comforts and $5 for clothes. It requires no extended argument on my part to convince the minister that $5 a month in 1936 was worth a good deal more than $5 a month is today. All that has been brought out in the veterans affairs committee and in the prices committee. A lot of these old veterans are chronic cases who will probably finish their days in these hospitals; and, as I say, they are receiving only $5 a month for comforts, for such things as cigarettes, toothpaste, and a lot of other little things that help to make their lives happier. There is another $5 a month available for clothes but that $5 is put away in their clothing account.
I rise this afternoon to protest against any pensioner of Canada or any soldier with meritorious service sufficient to entitle him to the war veterans allowance spending the rest of his days in hospital with an allowance of only $5 a month to buy the ordinary small comforts of life. I feel very strongly that the minister's department is placing these old veterans and the younger veterans of world war II in an impossible position in allowing them only $5 a month for comforts, and that a change in the regulations is imperative. The first change I would recommend would be that the minister bring the rates back to what they

were before they were changed in 1936. If the minister cannot do that he could at least make $10 a month available to the veteran to use as he sees fit. If the minister cannot do that, he could at least raise the amount available for comforts just as pensions and the vTar veterans allowance have been raised on the recommendation of the veterans committee.
I did not realize that there had been a reduction in the amount allowed for clothing and comforts. However I shall be glad to look into the matter.
I am taking my information from a veteran. Of course I may be wrong.

I will check on it. Leaving aside for the moment that question, and without attempting in any way to argue whether $5 a month is enough for comforts for these older men, I should like to say how greatly encouraged I was during the last few w'eeks in visiting some of these homes in the western part of our country, in Winnipeg, in Saskatchewan at the former lieutenant governor's home, and in Vancouver and Victoria. I think I talked with ninety per cent of the men who were resident there. It may have been kindness or politeness, but l must say that none of them raised the point noiv raised by my hon. friend. It may be it was something that they did not want to raise.
But leaving that aside as something to look into, I can assure the committee that the conditions under which these veterans were living were such as to make one's heart glad. Old men who would never be able to work were receiving attention and care from charming nurses and visits from the people of the community, and while I was in one hospital, a group of veterans were listening with great gusto to a boxing match coming over the radio, and showing every sign of living a life of contentment during a period of their years when they were no longer able to work. I am free to admit that there are others who are able and anxious to work, and we are prepared to help them gain that opportunity through the national employment service. I will take the point raised by my hon. friend into consideration and see what can be done.

With what the minister has had to say in regard to the hospitals, I must agree in large measure. They are ably staffed, and the people who are in charge of most of them are experienced in their work and do a tremendous amount to make the days of these old veterans of Canada as happy as possible. I am expressing today what may be the only remaining irritation of these veterans. It may seem a trifling matter to the government with

Supply-Veterans Affairs
a budget surplus of half a million dollars, but these old soldiers are forced to pinch and scrape on the little pocket-money they are allowed, and their lives would be made much happier if a larger allowance were made for comforts.

There are places in Canada where every once in a while a veteran is transferred from a military to a civilian hospital. In a case like that, how much does the department pay to the civilian hospital in ward rates?
I am told that the average would be $6.70, and we provide the medical service.
Under what terms are imperial soldiers admitted into D.V.A. hospitals?
If they are in receipt of a Canadian pension or war veterans allowance they are treated exactly the same as Canadians.
If they are in receipt of an imperial pension, under certain conditions they are admitted into D.V.A. hospitals.
Not unless that imperial pension is augmented by our Canadian pension, indicating that they were domiciled in Canada, but not if it is imperial pension alone.

I should like the minister to be quite certain that that answer is correct. Suppose a British pensioner has an ailment which is attributed to his service, and that pensioner is living in Canada; can he not be admitted into our D.V.A. hospitals?
If it is a British pension entirely? I understand that there are cases where we do take them in for treatment and all purposes, but at the cost of the British pension commission.
That is what I was asking. Their hospitalization is paid by the British ministry. Permission has to be obtained from the high commissioner's office here, I presume, or whatever office it is.

The British ministry of
pensions.
Then they are admitted into our hospitals. Are they charged at the rate of $9 a day?
They are charged at the standard rates of the hospital, if it is $9. Under the other arrangement it would be $9.
That would be paid by the British authorities.
Yes.

I notice that there is no classification of seamstresses in the details. Recently such a classification was adopted by hospitals run by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The department has classifications for housekeepers and waitresses. It is quite obvious that seamstresses are required in our veterans hospitals exactly as they are required in hospitals conducted by the Department of National Health and Welfare. Until recently they were paying their seamstresses', waitresses' or housemaids' pay in the Department of National Health and Welfare. I suggest that we need seamstresses. Can the minister say whether seamstresses are employed, and if so what rate are they paid, because I do not see it in the list of details?
I believe we have seamstresses, but I do not know how they are classified here. May I refer to that later?

Yes, if you would, because I do not think you will find it. They should be paid more than the rate paid for ordinary maid service. They should be paid on the same basis as the Department of National Health and Welfare pays.
I will get the information.

I have one complaint to make which has not been mentioned so far this afternoon. Some months ago enabling orders were issued by D.V.A. headquarters to permit the employment of optometrists on the staffs of D.V.A. hospitals and in clinics dealing with veterans' cases. Up to the moment, to the best of my knowledge, not one optometrist has been employed'. Are any being employed? These services are now being performed by ophthalmologists, and they are jealous of their position. My point is this. The ophthalmologist makes the examination and the optician fills the prescription. If some optometrists were employed by the department they would make the examination, fill the prescription and be responsible for it. I know that in many cases today chaps are getting the wrong lenses. I am not saying who is to blame. I feel it would be far more businesslike for the optometrist, the man who makes the examination, to fill the prescription and be responsible for it.
I thank the hon. member for Wentworth for his suggestion. I shall be glad to look into it.

I have one further word on the treatment sidle, and I wish to bring it to the attention of the minister. I do not intend to mention any names, but I have in mind five cases in which veterans suffering from some kind of war neurosis have had great difficulty
Supply-Veterans Affairs

in getting assistance from the Department of Veterans Affairs. I refer to an article, one of the last written by Kenneth Cragg, of the Globe and Mail, datelined Ottawa, January 30. In this article Mr.. Cragg mentions that in the view of the Department of Veterans Affairs pensions should foe allowed only in rare and fairly well-defined instances. He goes on to say that if you grant a pension to a neurotic you may handicap him for life. I understand from the hon. member for Lanark that this is also the view of the United) States government and of the British government. Therefore I have no quarrel with that view in a medical way, because I would not be well enough informed to quarrel with it.
The point I wish to make is a very simple one. These men are genuinely suffering from a war disability. It may be true that to pension them would do more harm than it would good, but there is one thing to which they should foe entitled. I suppose it would require a new definition in the Department of Veterans Affairs. They should foe entitled to treatment and hospitalization, when their parents, their wives or their families, or even they themselves, request it. That seems to me to be the least that we can do for a man who has a disability aggravated or caused in part or in whole by the war. He should be admitted to a veterans hospital, because he should receive a category which will make it possible for him to be admitted to any veterans hospital in Canada.
I have had experience in trying to get two of these men into hospital. They had nothing on their records. They were not sick. They were discharged fit, and all the rest of it; yet they had a history of neurosis in the services which in some cases was quite severe. There is the family background in both cases. It was very sad and compelling. I do not want to go into it. In the one case the hon. member for Wellington South and I were forced to co-operate in order to get a man into the hospital in London, Ontario. My only complaint or suggestion to the department in this instance is that some notation should be made on a veteran's document that he suffers from this type of illness or disability, so that he will have free access to our hospitals, should he require hospitalization.

I should like to say that the problem mentioned by the hon. member is one that our medical people recognize fully. I know of cases myself which come within that category, and we are attempting to find something like an answer.
I make the suggestion.

I have something I wish to bring to the attention of the minister under this item, and perhaps it is involved in item 537. It has to do with the Canadians who enlisted in the Belgian army. I believe there are about two or three hundred of these Canadian citizens who fought in the last great war.
One case that has been brought to my attention is that of a young veteran who was hospitalized for tuberculosis after the war. I managed to have his hospitalization taken care of, but he has been suffering from ill health ever since. Since the Department of Veterans Affairs does not pay a pension until the Belgian office is ready to pay their pension-in which case the Canadian veterans affairs department will supplement that pension-the situation is that this young veteran has no income. He is invalided. His only way or means of obtaining a livelihood is by remaining at home. Since two or three hundred other veterans might be in this situation, I should like the minister to comment on it. Can anything be done to hasten payment by the Belgian office? I have been in communication with the Belgian office on several different occasions trying to get some action on this matter, but have had no success.
I will consider that matter under item 537. Offhand I do not see that there is anything we could do except attempting to hasten payment. But I will check on the matter and give a further reply.

Item agreed to.
536. Prosthetic services, $952,584.

I should like to ask the minister what the situation is now with regard to the provision of hearing aids. I know that not so long ago the veteran who needed a hearing aid was provided with a certain one that the department had apparently adopted. That was the only one he could get, whether it fitted him, whether he thought it worked properly or whether it was any good to him or not. I know that a change has been made in regard to the matter, and I think the veteran who requires a hearing aid now has more choice. But I do not know whether he yet has a more or less full choice among the various types of equipment. Will the minister say just what the situation is?

The situation now is that the veteran has his own choice. If his choice should be for equipment that our people know is not a good kind, they will tell him so. But with that proviso, under counselling they have their free choice.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
537. Administration expenses, including chairman of the Canadian pension commission at $1,000 and the deputy chairman of the Canadian pension commission at $500 additional to chapter 62, statutes of 1946, $2,364,452'.

I wish to ask the minister this more or less general question. I understand that representations have now been made on behalf of the Canadian merchant marine. Can the minister say whether or not the department now has any set policy with respect to consideration for the Canadian merchant marine?

That was one of the points on which item 532, general departmental administration, was allowed to stand. That matter has been fully discussed by the parliamentary committee, and it would be premature for me to discuss it here before the committee submits its report. But there will be opportunity to discuss it later.
Will the minister comment on the question I just asked?
Perhaps it might stand until a little later.

Item agreed to.
539. War veterans allowance board-administration, $229,903.
I have a case in which a veteran is entitled to a burnt-out pension, I imagine you would call it, or veterans pension.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Veterans allowance.

Yes. But he has a sister whom he has kept for some twenty-five or thirty years. This man has a small bank account, and he is trying to keep it so that he can look after his sister and bury her. But he cannot get the veterans allowance until such time as he gets rid of this money. He could easily go out and spend it overnight, but he does not want to do that. I suppose he could give it away and then come under the allowance. Is there any way in which this man could come under the veterans allowance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: How much money has he?
About S3.000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: He has $1,800 too much.
The act was to provide for people who were in necessity and without means of support. The amount mentioned would be in excess of the amount that would enable us to do anything for him
Suppose this man went out and gave a part of that money away. What happens then? Is he entitled to the allowance?

I think it would be necessary for our officers to say that, if he considered that he could give that money away, he did not have any necessity for it; and consequently that he would not be in necessity in that particular situation.
That is what I was afraid of. Could he give the money to his sister, to look after her?

The deputy minister quotes the words, that if he rids himself of the property for the purpose of entitling him to come under the act, he would not be eligible. The matter of intention would enter into it, as it does in so many things.

Item agreed to.
5i0. Veterans' insurance, $98,329.
Will the minister explain briefly the purpose of this insurance? Is it to assist veterans to take out life insurance without a medical examination?

It is to enable veterans to get insurance who may be in a less robust physical condition than normal people. There are some occasions on which a medical examination may be required, but in most cases it is not.

Can the minister say why veterans who served in the allied forces, who are allowed practically every other benefit under the veterans legislation, are prohibited from taking advantage of this insurance?
As it stands now, if they are in receipt of a pension they may be eligible for insurance. As to the other question, I do not know whether that was taken up in the veterans affairs committee or not.

It has not been taken up in the veterans affairs committee. That is why I raised it here. Those veterans are entitled to practically every other veterans benefit, with some slight modifications; yet they are debarred from taking advantage of this insurance. I am referring to those veterans who were domiciled in Canada before the war, who fought with an allied force, then came back and are now domiciled in Canada. To all intents and purposes they are Canadians. Why should they not have the benefit of this insurance legislation in exactly the same way as any other Canadian has?

If there should be any demand in that field, the matter might be considered.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

May it be considered now? Will the minister take it into consideration? Will he refer it to the committee on veterans affairs either now or in the future? This seems to me to be an unfair restriction.
I shall be glad to consider it.
Will the minister say whether or not veterans insurance is strictly a government enterprise, or are policies underwritten by Canadian life insurance companies?
It is entirely and strictly a government enterprise.

Item agreed to.
Payments to or for veterans and dependents-
5hl- Pensions for disability and death, including pensions granted under the authority of the civilian government employees (war) compensation order P.C. 45/8848 of 22nd November, 1944, which shall be subject to the Pension Act, $80,014,000.

What are the latest figures on applications for pension which have been turned down on the ground that the applicant was suffering from a pre-enlistment condition not aggravated? In the veterans affaire committee in 1946 we were given figures up to December 31, 1945, and they showed that, of veterans who had service in a theatre of actual war outside Canada, 7,810 had been refused pension on the ground that their disability was pre-enlistment and not aggravated, and that, of those with service wholly in Canada, the figure was 54,207. Last year I got figures up to June 30, 1947, and they showed that of those witli service in a theatre of war, the number was 13,321, and service wholly in Canada, 72,340. That was a total of 85,661 whose application for pension had been refused on the ground that they were suffering from a pre-enlistment condition not aggravated. Can the minister give us any- later figures? It will be noticed that the last figures are up to June 30, 1947.
We have no figures later than those, but we could obtain them up to the beginning of 1948. I understand that there would not be a great increase at the present time.
They can be got up to the end of 1947?
Yes.
I would ask that that be done.
Perhaps under the item that has been allowed to stand.

There is one class of men who should have entitlement, and that is those

who adopted children after the pensionable injury occurred. Usually children are adopted for very good reasons, and certainly not with a view to obtaining the few additional dollars that might be received in the way of pension. Suppose a pensioner is unable to have children naturally and wishes to adopt a child. If the local authorities consider him of sufficiently good character, a man of good calibre, to entrust him with the upbringing of a child, the pension commission turn him down if the adoption took place after the pensionable injury occurred. That is something which certainly does not take place where the child is the natural offspring of the pensioner, even if it is bom after the injury has been sustained. This is a class who, in my opinion, should receive serious consideration by the department.

I have one question to ask the minister and I think it will be of general interest to the committee. An English subject enlisted with the Canadian army overseas. He served with the Canadian army, later married, now has two children, and is a 100 per cent disability case, receiving his cheque regularly from the Canadian government. He now seeks admission to Canada. Is there anything to prevent his coming to Canada?
Does my hon. friend mean, if he comes to Canada will he lose his pension?
No. The question is, can he come to Canada? He has never been able to come here.

By virtue of his service in the Canadian army, one would think he would be a Canadian citizen, but that would be a matter entirely within the jurisdiction of the immigration authorities, and I would not care to make a comment.
I am bringing up the question because I think it is of interest to the committee generally.
In that connection. I should think this would be a matter for the Department of Veterans Affairs to take up with the immigration authorities.
I was going to add that. If the hon. member will give me the facts of the case I shall try to unravel it.

Has the department considered any provision for a man who served at least five years overseas, without any black marks against him, and who now finds himself in the position where he is unable to hold a job, his condition appearing to have been preenlistment? Is there any provision for such chaps? This man served five years overseas.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
and he cannot now hold a job owing to his disability, the department claiming that it is pre-enlistment. He had no black marks against him during his five years of service. Surely he deserves consideration now.

It was for such veterans that special arrangements were made under the War Veterans Allowance Act. His physical condition now, which is non-pensionable, is due to a pre-enlistment disorder, and for that reason he is unemployable. He should make application for war veterans allowance, regardless of his age, if he had service outside Canada in the last war.

In view of the amendment passed, to section 11 1(c), striking out the words "wilfully and deliberately concealed", will a review be made of those cases where pension was refused on the ground that the applicant had wilfully concealed disability at the time of enlistment?
That is under way now.
Upon application only?
Yes.

Why should it be necessary for the veteran to apply? There will be thousands of these veterans who will never know that they can apply. One good illustration of the difficulty in that connection is the trouble which the minister's colleague, the Minister of Finance, or perhaps it is the Minister of National Revenue, is having in locating people who have refundable savings coming to them. One would suppose that every person having refundable savings payable to him would let the department know of his whereabouts, but apparently there are thousands of such persons who are not communicating with the department. The same is true of veterans. There wall be veterans in places all over Canada who will never learn that they can get pension in consequence of the change in the section, and I suggest that in all cases in which pension has been refused there should be a review automatically by the pension commission and the pensions granted without the commission sitting back and waiting for the veteran to apply. It is most unfair to hold out on the veteran in that way.

In the matter of making known those changes that have been made in all veterans legislation this session, as soon as the session closes there will be a conference on the part of my officials for the purpose of publishing a summary, and also working out plans which we feel can best carry out the letter and spirit of those amendments, along the lines mentioned here. I can assure hon.
members that no effort will be spared to attempt to interpret those amendments in the best possible way.

The minister will recall
that during the earlier discussions of the special committee there was agreement to recommend to the department that meritorious pensions granted under section 21, should be automatically increased without its being necessary to wait for an application from the pensioner. I am sure that all members who served on the committee would like to have cases which will benefit by the other changes dealt with automatically in the same way, without the necessity of having to wait for applications to be made. If there are other amendments to the act benefiting veterans, then I think those benefits should go out automatically. Such cases should be dealt with automatically, and there should be no need to wait for an application.

I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South. It would be much simpler to do it on an automatic basis than to wait for applications. There is no question that many veterans will never know this legislation has been passed. As we go across the country, we find that many statutes with which one would think people would be familiar, and which have been given publicity, are not well known. There will be many cases where veterans have been denied pensions on the ground that their disabilities were of preenlistment origin. That veteran may still be denied later on, on the ground that it was recorded. I suggest, therefore, that in every case where the pension commission have a file of a list of soldiers or veterans who were denied pensions on the ground that for a time they wilfully concealed their disability, those cases should be taken up and reviewed. There will be some cases where disabilities may have been recorded, and where veterans would not be eligible for pensions.

Since I was not a member of the special committee on veterans affairs I hesitate to say anything here, because there are so many other members quite capable of dealing with the matter. However I would associate myself with the hon. members for Vancouver South and Acadia in what they have said this afternoon. It seems to me that where an improvement has been made in the Pension Act or in the War Veterans Allowance Act, where it is on record that a person would be entitled to the improved benefits of the act, the department should not wait for the individuals concerned to make applications. Those cases should now be taken up automatically by the department. They
Supply-Veterans Affairs

should be advised that they are now eligible for the improved pension or allowance, as the case may be.

I can assure hon. members who have spoken that the object they have in mind is exactly that of the department. Perhaps it has been overlooked, but steps will be taken to do what is desired. The point is this: Is it better for us now to go into files which have been semi-dead, when we have pensions advocates who have under their care cases such as those we have been discussing and who have been bringing them back for review by the pension board. It is a case of having to decide, as I think we must, which appears to us to require priority, to accomplish what has been mentioned this afternoon.

Rut there are only a handful of pensions advocates across the country. They will be working with a very small number of these cases in which pensions have been refused on certain grounds which have now been removed. There will be only a handful of those cases on the desks of the pensions advocates. If the department does not move to grant the pensions it may be years before these veterans receive any benefit from the legislation. I suggest that a staff should be put to work in the Department of Veterans Affairs right away to go over these cases which have been turned down, and to arrange that the veterans receive the benefits.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There is one other point I should like to bring to the minister's attention. As the minister recalls, in respect of the increase both in the disability pension and in the war veterans allowance, it has been made clear that those amounts will be paid automatically. On the basis of that information I have answered letters telling veterans that they do not have to apply for those adjustments, but they need only bide their time and the adjustments will be made. It seems to me that the effect of that will carry over into this stage of the matter as well. Veterans generally will tend to feel that it is automatic, and they will not apply until they discover that it is not.
Surely veterans bureaux or veterans advocates will not have complete files of cases where veterans have been denied pensions on the ground that disability was wilfully concealed.

Complete files will be available. But I can assure hon. members that this discussion will be kept carefully in mind in working out the plans to review these cases.

May I reply to a question asked about Canadian ex-servicemen who served with the Belgian forces? They may have their pension awards increased to Canadian rates. They must establish entitlement, and obtain the original award from the country with which they served. There are very few Belgian cases in which decisions have not been rendered. The number is small.
Are the service bureaux and adjustment offices of the Canadian Legion being supported by the government?

The veterans bureau is a service provided by the department at public expense on behalf of the veterans. Twelve or fifteen years ago it was decided that it was not desirable to instruct the veteran that he must, as a compulsory matter, come to a government advocate, no matter how impartial that advocate might be. It was made optional that he could go to a veterans' organization to receive help and advice in preparing his case.

The reason for my question is that I have had some dealings with the service bureau in the Hamilton district, and with satisfactory results. I believe these service bureaux officers are taking a great interest in veterans' cases, and they are not now being left to pensions advocates. That has been my experience. The service bureau officer in Hamilton is doing a splendid job. This bureau is replacing the old system of pensions advocates who sometimes were not taking the interest they should in cases. If these cases are dealt- with in the manner in which they are in Hamilton I think the situation will be much better in the future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: To revert to the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South about section 21, the situation with respect to a pension granted under that section is that more than half of those in receipt of pension have already-been reviewed; tihe review is proceeding without request from the recipients.
What we are suggesting is that the same procedure be followed in the case of men who have been ruled out because of pre-enlistment conditions.

Are these Belgian soldier cases being handled with dispatch, -or is there any reason why there should be delay in particular cases? In the case I have before me the veteran had to wait for over two years before settlement was made. The answer -that is always given is that the Belgian office is the cause of the delay. Will it be possible to correct this situation in the near

I took this matter up in the house two years ago and have had considerable correspondence about it with the department. It is becoming an increasingly serious question to certain settlers in Alberta because of the extension of the oil fields there. The situation has been that even when the soldier settler had paid for his land in full and got possession the board reserved the mineral rights, although in many cases the soldier thought he was buying the mineral rights as well as the surface rights to his property. An amendment to the Soldier Settlement Act was introduced in this house some years ago to deal with this matter, but it was defeated in the other place. The

previous minister of veterans affairs intimated to me some time ago that he thought probably that amendment should be reintroduced and the matter fixed up in that way. Is any consideration being given to that, and would the government be prepared to reintroduce an amendment?

I know that a great number of members from the west are interested in this matter. My attention was called to it shortly after I came into this department. We have been taking the matter up in close cooperation with the Department of Mines and Resources, and we have even got to the point of putting forward what appears to be a possible solution for the consideration of the Department of Justice. We will follow that up as soon as we get a ruling from the justice department on the points raised. I am familiar with the history of the former bill which passed this house and died in another place. It ought to be possible by next session, if not before, to bring the matter forward.

Is it not possible to get around the difficulty without having an amendment to the law? In other words, is that what you have referred to the Department of Justice for a ruling? Or is it still considered necessary to amend the act?
If we find that an amendment to the act is not necessary we shall be very happy to carry the plan into effect as suggested.
I shall be glad to follow that suggestion, because the opportunity is still there for those eligible from world war II, since no limitation is yet placed upon the time.
I ask the minister if he would give greater publicity to it, so that veterans who are not aware of it may profit from it.
I shall be glad to do that.

With respect to the question of mineral rights which was taken up a few moments ago by the hon. member for Calgary East, I may say I have been playing around with this on behalf of my constituents for nearly two years. Apparently two or three departments of government have been playing around with it also. Since coming here last December, I have discussed the matter on various occasions with the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Only a couple of days ago he told me to come in to see him on Monday next. That is the reason I have not taken the matter up with him today. I have been assured by the minister that we are nearing an agreement. If that agreement is not reached satisfactorily I can tell the minister that we shall have some more playing around with this question.
I understand that up to 1883 mineral rights went with the land. Since that time, the lights have been reserved by the crown. In many cases, 1,200 or 1,300 I believe, settlers who took out lands under the soldier settlement board did get the mineral rights on their land. Section 57 of the Soldier Settlement Act took away or confiscated these mineral rights. In 1940 the government saw fit to bring in a bill, No. 31, which was passed through this house without very much discussion. However, when it went to the other place there was some discussion there as to the right of a farmer to have mineral rights. The final decision arrived at was that farmers were placed on the land by the soldier settlement board primarily for the purpose of farming, and as a result of that they were not entitled to mineral rights. The soldier settlement board might just as well confiscate buildings and other improvements on a farm as confiscate the mineral rights.
My constituency is vitally interested in this question because we have a lot of oil in the Llovdminster, Vermilion, Wainwright and other districts in that constituency. While a number of our soldier settlers are interested, I feel that the time is close at hand when the
5849-347i
government will see fit to return to these people that which they confiscated from them by section 57 of the Soldier Settlement Act.
I am not pressing this question at the present time, because the minister, in whom I have every confidence, told me to see him again next week. I am hoping at that time to get a satisfactory reply from him, but I assure the minister now and the government that unless some satisfactory settlement is made of this, that is, giving back to the soldier settlers that which was confiscated from them, we shall have some lawsuits and some more playing around through the courts, because we have been playing around long enough with the department and with the government.

The statement follows: Discrimination against certain areas of the province of Saskatchewan. In the purchase of land for veterans the department makes no discrimination in regard to any particular area in Canada, but great care is exercised to ensure that veterans are not established on marginal or submarginal farm land. Any deviation from this policy, even for the strongest sentimental reasons, would not be in keeping with the spirit and intent of the Veterans' Land Act. It has always been the policy of the department to assist veterans to re-establish themselves in civil life on a sound, long-term basis. Anything less would be playing false to those to whom Canada owes so much.
However, to be more specific, as far back as July, 1943, a policy was laid down after consultation with senior agricultural officials of the provincial departments of the prairie provinces and the western universities, and a number of outstanding farmers. The departmental officials had had extensive experience settling veterans of world war I, and were well aware of pitfalls to be avoided.
Briefly, that policy restricts land purchases to certain types of soil in different areas,
Supply-Veterans Affairs

depending on climatic conditions. It was formulated after an exhaustive study of all available information with regard to longterm crop yields, bonuses under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, relief records, soil textures, and fertility and precipitation data.
In practice, each field supervisor is provided with soil survey report No. 12 for the province of Saskatchewan, and up-to-date soil maps. The survey report gives a comprehensive description of the soils of the provinces, discusses their limitations for agricultural use, and contains a soil rating index for each soil type. Land appraisals are made with great care and include a careful examination of both top and sub-soils. Where available, aerial photographs are being distributed to assist the field supervisor to outline the physical features of the farm. Use is made of the economic land classification maps published by the economics division, Department of Agriculture, in co-operation with the department of farm management, University of Saskatchewan. In addition, the administration itself has records of long-term yields and data concerning yield variations in particular areas. Even with all this information available it is again pointed out that under present policy no farm is turned down until it has been individually examined and considered strictly on its own merits as an economic unit, and in relation to the price asked.
Thus, when a farm is declared unsuitable, having been considered from all these points of view, the administration would indeed be false to its trust if it were to permit a veteran to make what is probably the one big purchase of his lifetime on such a property, however much the veteran himself may desire to locate there at that particular time. In fact, instances have occurred when veterans subsequently established on sound propositions have expressed sincere gratitude for having been saved from the pitfalls of settlement on an uneconomic unit.
With respect to settlement in the hon. member for Lake Centre's constituency a map indicates that veterans have been settled on parcels of land uniformly dispersed and comparable to almost any other section of the province.
Reasons for declining purchase of certain parcels of land. Mr. Diefenbaker has quoted an extract from a letter forwarded by a departmental official to a veteran, in which the veteran was advised that the farm in question could not be purchased, and the reasons could not be given as they were strictly confidential. Admittedly, this was an unfortun-

ate letter, but it is certainly an isolated case. A recent survey of copies of letters declining purchase sent to veterans in Mr. Diefenbaker's constituency during the padt fifteen months indicates that the following extract is more typical:-
However, the committee did state that they considered the land unsuitable, and I think if you had looked over the farm, you would perhaps realize yourself just why it was rejected, especially if you compared it with a good farm in a good area. You can also have a very good idea of the type of farm it is by comparing the assessment with land which is of a good class. In this case, one quarter is assessed at $1,050 and the other at $1,000, and according to the assessment commission, ratings below $1,200 are considered sub-marginal.
It might be pointed out that initially it was a custom to state quite clearly to a veteran why a farm was unsuitable, but it was found that it was causing considerable embarrassment to the vendor and other individuals interested in the community. It was then decided that specific reasons should not be given in order that a vendor whose farm might represent his life's work would not have his property publicly condemned. Admittedly it is a choice of evils, but no doulbt the hon. member for Labe Centre would be very quick to champion the rights of individual citizens whose assets were being publicly depreciated by a government department.
Delays in obtaining approval for settlement. It is admitted that there were delays in the handling of applications for loans in the past, particularly in the fall of 1946 when the regional offices were swamped with applications just before freeze-up. It will be readily understood that accurate appraisals cannot be made during, winter months. It took six weeks to two months to catch up with this backlog in the spring of 1947. This year there was a very small backlog of applications on hand, but as the spring has been very late, with extremely bad roads, there was a hold-up in the appraisals in some areas until nearly the middle of May. The district superintendent for the province of Saskatchewan reported on June 4 that there were only twenty odd appraisals outstanding, and these are being checked rapidly. The district superintendent reported further that for current applications the time from the date of appraisal until the veteran is advised varies from five to twenty days, with the average time being approximately fourteen days.
Increase in the amount of loan as requested by the Govan Branch of the Canadian Legion. The resolution by some of the branches of the legion recommending an increase in the amount of loan to veterans being established under the

Supply-Veterans Affairs
Veterans' Land Act was turned down by the resolutions committee at the recent dominion convention of the Canadian Legion which was held in Saskatoon, as it was felt that to go beyond the present maximum of the act would be loading the veteran with too large a debt, and that it would be wiser to encourage establishment under section 9 (3) of the act, followed subsequently by an establishment under section 9 (1) when the veteran had sufficient funds of his own to supplement the loan in order to buy a more expensive unit.
Veterans settled on small holdings in Prince Albert. Mr. Diefenbaker made reference to eight veterans in the Prince Albert area who signed an agreement to purchase a small holding at a certain figure, and indicated that subsequently they were asked to sign another agreement at a higher figure. It is assumed that all eight cases are typical of the one specific case quoted, in which the circumstances are as follows:
This veteran was permitted occupancy before the house was completed and the actual cost known and, as he requested a loan for equipment, it was necessary that he sign an agreement for what was estimated would be the cost of the house. It will be recalled that at that time there was a heavy demand for housing. and for humanitarian reasons the department departed from normal practice and permitted veterans to occupy houses which were habitable but not completed. Subsequently, due to the increased cost of construction, it was found that the actual cost of the house had been under-estimated, and thus, in keeping with the act, it became necessary to request a new agreement at the increased figure.
The department feels justified in taking such humanitarian action, even though it has later caused some embarrassment both to the department and the veteran.
The obtaining of machinery for veterans. The hon. member for Lake Centre suggests that some provision should be made for priority in machinery for veterans. It is pointed out that this priority system exists at the present time and has for several years, and has been receiving the wholehearted cooperation of the machinery manufacturers and their dealers. For example, as of March 31 this year 8,731 tractors and 880 combines had been delivered to veterans since the inception of the act. In point of fact, veterans established under the Veterans Land Act are much better supplied with new implements than any other group of farmers in Canada. In Saskatchewan 68 per cent of the farmers have tractors of some kind, many of these twelve, thirteen and fourteen years old; 53-4 per cent of veterans being established have
new tractors, and approximately 20 per cent have second-hand tractors of one kind or another.
In order to acquaint the machinery companies with the expected requirements of machinery for veterans settling under the act, their estimated requirements are ascertained from district and regional offices approximately fifteen months before delivery is required. This information is carefully screened and a definite figure as to the quantities of the different models of machines required is established. Implement companies are then approached, and definite arrangements made with them to deliver to veterans coming under the act the machines so ordered at the price in effect at time of delivery, less 10 per cent on general line machines and 7 per cent on tractors and combines. Each year provision has been made to meet the estimated over-all requirements, but there have been many production difficulties which have prevented the implement companies from fulfilling their commitments. Whenever it became apparent that any types of machines had been ordered in excess of actual requirements, the surplus implements were immediately returned to the manufacture to be distributed amongst veterans establishing themselves, or to agriculture generally.
While there were no specific quantities arranged to meet the requirements of veterans establishing themselves outside the act, there has been in effect a working arrangement with implement companies to set aside a percentage of their total production to meet special orders coming from veterans who are establishing themselves and, in addition, when urgent requirements develop, machines are released, wherever possible, from Veterans' Land Act quotas.
Veterans with low disabilities denied settlement. It is certainly not the policy of the department to refuse assistance solely on the ground of a small disability. Already many veterans with high disabilities have been established as full-time farmers. Where any doubt does exist, however, as to the veteran's physical condition, the matter is referred to the medical profession for an opinion. These opinions are, of course, confidential, but if the hon. member for Lake Centre will supply the name of the veteran in question, whose total disability is 5 per cent and who has been declined settlement, the full facts of the case can be made available to him.
