On this question of departmental administration, I intended last night, when the hon. member for Lethbridge got the floor, to mention two or three small matters in connection with this vote. I will take the opportunity now and I promise you, Mr. Chairman, that I will not detain the committee for more than five or six minutes. I appreciate the work that has been done by the present minister as well as by his predecessor, evidence of which was visible in the international trade fair that we witnessed last week. It was a wonderful world's fair exhibition of our trade and commerce and I hope it will be an annual event.
The minister has effected some improvements in our trade with the mother country. In this connection, I should like to refer to an editorial that appeared in one of the local newspapers this morning, the Ottawa Citizen, in reference to something on trade I said the other night. I would suggest that it would be well if this newspaper could do something to promote the progress of its own city, as the city from which I come has progressed in different directions. This editorial did not quote one word of what I said on trade the other night with reference to preferential trade or the great loss that this country sustained when we tossed overboard valuable principles of trade in committing ourselves to Bretton Woods and the United States loan at Geneva in 1945. All the well-tried economic principles by which this country has progressed ever since confederation have been discarded. The other night I was simply trying to justify the national policy that has been responsible for the growth of commerce in Canada. I was not advocating the national policy of 1878. What I was advocating was a national policy for the living and not for the dead. The national policy, however, has done a great deal for Canada. It got us steady markets with our best customers, not north and south, but east and west. It got us markets throughout the world for our grain, foodstuffs and various other commodities.
I do not object to the criticism of any local newspaper, and I do not mind whether I am called Progressive, Liberal, or Conservative. They may call me whatsoever they like; they cannot say, nor have they ever said, one word against progressive measures I promoted here for many years. If they would get their own town to take some progressive steps it would be better. The city from which I come made progress twenty-five years ago in connection with the street railway, light, power and hydro, and if they would do the same for their own town in housing and in various-
Supply-Trade and Commerce

other municipal ways it would be better for all concerned. Fifteen to twenty years ago we saw the -wooden houses across the river, in Hull, when I was urging a national housing policy for this country and opposing the giveaway of power in 1927 in the Ottawa district.
Progress is what is wanted in this country today. What we want is progress and principle, not peanuts and party. That applies to our friends of the Citizen. One of their staff went to Japan and then founded the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Let them look after their own progress and never mind mine. As I said last night, I do not change my polities, nor do I veer from my principles. I have been in this house for a considerable time and have consistently advocated certain principles, and I stick to those principles whether I am in the house or out of it.
Regarding this particular department, I made reference the other night to certain improvements which I think can be effected, and I never referred to the Ontario election. I never mentioned it. What I did say was that a political party that sticks to its principles will never lack for a following, and a political party that has no principles will get nowhere. I was not referring to personalities but to the principle at stake. In the past, the party to which I belong has consistently followed economic principles of protection that have done a great deal for the country; our own work for our own workmen; our own markets for our own production. I admit, of course, that the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier also did a great deal for Canada, but did not alter the tariff much. I say that freely because I am not a hidebound party man; far from it. But I believe in certain mneiples of trade, certain economic principles 7hich in my opinion should be carried out l this country; and I do not believe that Sir Wilfrid Laurier departed very much, in atters of trade and commerce, from the lieies of his predecessors, f did not believe in union government, and Jo not now believe in the form of government that is in existence today in Manitoba and British Columbia. But that is none of my business; it is a matter for the electors of Manitoba and British Columbia respectively to choose their own government. I will say, however, that as a result of the policy in Manitoba and British Columbia there is but one alternative for a voter there, and that is the party of our hon. friends to the left.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I fully appreciate the
ability of my hon. friend, who is his party's whip. He is active in the house and is very likeable in many ways. For that matter, so are all my hon. friends to the left. But when it comes to principles of trade and commerce, I repeat, we of this party have never changed our ideas. They can call us anything they like, but we stand by our principles. I was too modest the other night to admit that I was a progressive, but I suggest that there could be greater progress in the city of Ottawa. It is badly needed. As regards a public utility here, the stock was 17; it is now 42J in the stock markets, and it is still going up.
Last fall I delivered an address to the pupils of one of our schools and I spoke somewhat in these terms: "Some of you will very soon find yourselves on the thorny path of public life. Do not forget, while paying the closest attention to the welfare of your constituents, the important principle that nothing that, anyone says should alter your own opinion of doing what you think is right." I said to those students to remember that the greatest crime that had been committed in all history was the crime perpetrated by one who paid too much heed to popular opinion and the populace, and that was Pontius Pilate. One fact that should be borne in mind by leaders in every walk of life, and by politicians the world over in these dangerous times is this. It is not cleverness but independence of character that counts, that independence of character which is so often lacking not only in our own country, among our own public men, but in many other countries the world over. It is the lack of that independence which has led to the present state of affairs. We find that politicians the world over tend to follow rather than to lead public opinion, for it is easy and more profitable to swim with the tide than against it. If you go against the tide you may be submerged.
I do not know that I have much more to say with reference to that article which commented upon what I had to say-without quoting a word of it-about trade and commerce. I have only this to say, that it would be far better if the leaders of all parties decided, instead of keeping their ear to the ground so much, to lead public opinion rather than follow it. That is the attitude we need. It is this cause and effect that loses elections.
I voted against Bretton Woods because I saw what was coming; I foresaw the disaster in connection with our dollar. I knew what the dollar situation would be. I also criticized the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
United States loan. In my opinion, we lost our best customer when we threw overboard the principles of preferential trade. By it, our province, more than any other, western Ontario particularly, did a great deal to improve trade between this country and Britain, as well as between Canada and all the other countries on the seven seas. Those hon. members who saw the magnificent exhibits in the international trade fair the other day at the exhibition grounds in Toronto must have rejoiced to see the extent to which the trade of Canada has been and could be developed with the sterling countries by empire trade.
I wish the present Minister of Trade and Commerce every success in his work, now that he has taken over this department. I recognize that he did a great deal of good work during the war. I appreciate that and I am fair enough to say it. He has worked hard and I hope he will be a success. I trust that as soon as he can he will rid this country of its austerity program, restore preferential empire trade, do what he can to rectify the dollar situation and give to the small businessman and the big businessman as well a chance to flourish and to conduct his business in his own way by free enterprise, which is very necessary at the present time.
I was sorry we did not stay in the sterling area, largely because people voted down these free trade and unrestricted reciprocity policies away back in 1911. Today we have nothing but unrestricted reciprocity, free trade with the United States. So much is this true that Time magazine, which I quoted recently, said that we are becoming the 49th state of the union.
These are very involved matters for trade and commerce. This is the 109th day of the session. It has been a strenuous session and the minister has worked hard. All the ministers have done that. I appreciate the fact that we have in this party today a party which has given the government substantial aid and support since last December. I hope that we shall have a recess from our duties beginning next Friday night, and that the government of today will see to it that as soon as they can they will restore preferential trade with our best customers, the mother country and the dominions. After all is said and done, that is where the cream of our trade is-and when I say that I refer to trade in manufactured goods, food and other raw commodities.
The resources of Great Britain and her dominions both in manufactured goods and in raw materials are far greater than those of Russia or the United States. As was said by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir John A. Macdonald, the mother country, with the dominions, is our best customer. And there has not been much change in policy since the days of those statesmen. We might add the countries of Europe which were with us in the first war, and which served as a market for our grain and other food products.
I rejoiced to see the exhibition in Toronto recently, because I know it will restore much of the trade we had with the sterling countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I should like to say this to
the hon. member for Broadview. I have sat in the house with him for a good many years and he has been here longer than I have. I believe the hon. member has made something of a record in the public life of this country, in that he is impervious to newspaper or any other kind of criticism. He has shown many acts of kindness and done many constructive acts of statesmanship in both municipal and dominion affairs. We know where he stands. He stands for the city from which he comes and for the community he represents. I hope he will be with us for a good many years to come.

A short time ago the minister mentioned that goods to the value of
8400.000	were to go to Czechoslovakia. Are they still going forward? Has there been any change?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Such orders as are placed are going forward. It is about 8400,000, I believe.
What arrangements have been made for collecting that debt?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Payments are being made when due.
Will the minister make his announcement respecting the United States motion picture industry under the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce or those of Reconstruction and Supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I have nothing much to add to my previous statement.
The minister said he would make an announcement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I hope to be able to reduce it to paper, but I have not done so yet. Arrangements have been made for a considerable amount of Canadian publicity to be put out at the expense and through the agency of the moving picture industry. Certain shorts have been made by the industry and a few by the government of Canada which are being circulated through United States outlets. A comprehensive plan has been studied and partly
Supply-Trade and Commerce

agreed upon. I am not in a position to announce it today; I wish I were. I think hon. members will agree however that Canada is getting good value for the exchange privileges being allowed the industry in this country.

Last night the minister gave figures with regard to trade between Canada and the United States and between Canada and the United Kingdom. No mention was made of trade between Canada and Australia and New Zealand. On the Pacific coast we are interested in that trade. Would the minister give us some information with regard to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The only 1948 figures I have are for our two principal customers, the United States and the United Kingdom. I believe I have the 1947 figures for other trade. The position of trade with Australia and New Zealand is that their imports are being reduced substantially by an austerity program very much like that of England. Certain dollar funds are allocated to Canada, and imports are cut back to keep within the over-all allocation. However, we are shipping the usual exports to Australia and New Zealand, although in smaller quantities than was the case previously. Exports to British dominions, which would be largely Australia, New' Zealand and South Africa, stood at $17,300,000 a month, average shipments. In 1946 the figure was $14,300,000. Exports to Australia in 1947, I find, were $60,294,201, and imports in that year were $14,222,487. Those are the largest exports on record, and the rate of imports is about the average.

I am keenly interested in this, because about a month ago there was a press dispatch reporting a submission that was made to the government by the Canadian exporters' association. The dispatch is dated at Toronto, May 17, and states:
The Canadian exporters' association, in a submission to trade minister Howe, said that the falling-off of export sales to British empire markets is so alarming that steps should be taken to counteract it. Canada, the submission says, finds herself in the peculiar position of being the sole member of the British commonwealth unable to trade more or less freely in empire markets which have become increasingly important to Canada in the development of our world trade.
Then the dispatch goes on to say:
Unless some action is taken with alacrity Canadian exporters feel that they might be faced with the permanent loss of the empire markets.
Would the minister make a comment on that dispatch? If conditions are that serious, are any steps being taken by the government to meet the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Our exports to empire markets at the present time are, I believe, running the highest in peacetime history. There is a cutting back of manufactured goods. That has been noticed by exporters who are interested in manufactured goods. When Canada ran into dollar difficulties the first thing that was cut off was manufactured goods such as automobiles and goods of that kind. It is the same in Australia and New Zealand. As a rule, the cut comes in manufactured goods of the semiluxury type. Those industries are feeling it badly, just as are the people who are accustomed to ship to Canada. But our over-all export position to British countries is good.

Is it not true that
Australia became industrialized during the war and is now producing to a substantial extent many of the commodities that it previously bought in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is true, but not to an extent that would interfere abnormally with Canadian exports. Usually, when new lines are opened up it really stimulates exports from other countries rather than the opposite. The difficulty in Australia at the moment is a lack of dollars and a strict limitation of the expenditure of dollars on this continent.
When the minister speaks of our export trade and its volume he is including our export trade to Great Britain, much of which is on Canadian credits.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We include exports to Great Britain, because Great Britain is our second largest market. We include exports to South Africa, India, Australia, New Zealand and the British West Indies. The only serious drop is in our exports to Australia and New Zealand and: the British West Indies, and in those cases the drop is chiefly in manufactured goods, although they are also buying less lumber and other raw materials than formerly.
If we exclude or write off the credits, has there been a drop in purchasing by Great Britain as compared with before the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Britain is not drawing on credits at the moment.
She has been, according to the figures the minister gave.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
She was drawing until the middle of April; in that period the total was $52,500,000. At the moment they are not drawing on credits. We cannot say when they will resume, but it may be just as soon as our financial position permits.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Has any attempt been made to improve our trade with Australia and New Zealand? 13 there any way by which Canada can help them overcome their shortage of Canadian dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not know of any. We are most anxious to buy anything from Australia and New Zealand that they can ship. We have actually promoted imports from those two countries, but there is only a limited amount of goods that they can ship here. If they could ship sugar it would help a great deal, but all the sugar goes to the United Kingdom. Anything that we can buy there we are buying. Of course that is the only real way to build up trade under conditions such as we have today. The balance of trade is very much in our favour.
Fourteen million dollars as against 860,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: About that.

The people on the Pacific coast are also interested in trade with China. I understand that there have been some difficulties in opening up that trade and the people on the coast are complaining. What is the trouble there?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Nothing is coming out of China; exports are almost nil. As my hon. friends know, China is suffering from an unlimited inflation and civil war and production has just dropped to negligible proportions.
Are any goods going from Canada to China?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: In 1947 we exported nearly $35,000,000 worth and we imported from China $2,300,000 worth.

There is something more important- than trade with China and the Fiji islands or other countries that cannot send exports to Canada. I refer to our whole trade policy. I pay a tribute to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am ready to stand by him to the limit, because I consider that his task at the present time is vital for the welfare of this country, provided that trade is real and not imaginary.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Stanstead in the questions he has asked with regard to the trade policies of this government. During the war it was impossible for me to find out what exports were being paid for and what exports we were paying for ourselves. That sort of trade was a false trade; it was not trade at all. Santa Claus does not trade with anybody, he gives things away to children. He cannot be called a general merchant
or a businessman. Santa Claus is a giver, and Canada was acting as Santa Claus to the United Kingdom during and after the war.
I do not consider that trade financed by credits which are obtained by taxation is real trade. Our trade policy should be realistic. If countries have not the currency to purchase our products, let us get their goods. Let us trade with all countries in the world that have goods to send us. Let us exchange goods; let us barter goods, and then we can consider paying the difference with some kind of currency.
The idea of trade within the British empire is detrimental to real trade. In matters of trade England is not a friend; the United States is not a friend; France is not a friend; they are all competitors. If Canada has not the ability to sell her products in competition with those of England, to discuss with everybody the purchase of Canadian goods in preference to British goods, then it is useless to have a Department of Trade and Commerce. If Canada in matters of trade is to be like the little porpoise attached to the mother porpoise and following her through the seven seas, then let us abandon the discussion of trade and admit that we are just serfs without dignity, that we are not interested in the welfare and progress of this country.
Why do we have British preference conferences? They were just reminders of the old colonial trade policy when it was forbidden to Canada to trade with any country except England. When those barriers disappeared we had free trade with the United States, during which time Canada was more prosperous than she had ever been before or has been since. Why are we not realistic with regard to trade? Why do we think we have to trade only under the shade of Great Britain? Why do we not give every possible encouragement to our own trade commissioners and consuls general and free them from the influence of the United Kingdom ambassadors? One of the great errors made by the Prime Minister was when he said, at the time the consulate general was set up in New York, that the consul general would confer with the British consul general. What a mistake. Is there any other country in the world that does the same thing? Australia competes with England; New Zealand competes with England; South Africa competes with England. Every country, except small islands in the Caribbean seas or the South seas, is bold enough to face England and fight her in the markets of the world, and by doing that they are more respected by the merchants of London and Manchester and other English manufacturing centres than are the bloated colonials we have here who think
Supply-Trade and Commerce

we should creep under the petticoats of Britain to trade on the markets of the world.
Let us be realistic. I want the Minister of Trade and Commerce to be the big boss of his department, just as I want the minister of external affairs to be the big boss of his department. But the purposes of the two departments are entirely different. The aim of the Department of External Affairs is to keep Canada at peace with all the countries of the world, and the aim of the Minister of Trade and Commerce should be to boost the trade of Canada against every competitor, British, American, French, Japanese or that of any other country.
We should stop that false banking policy of advancing money to those who are to buy from us. It is the Canadian taxpayer who pays for these goods, and now our taxes are piled high just on account of those gifts that I was one of the few in this house to denounce during the war, for they were perfectly nonsensical. The Conservative party then led by the former member for York-Sunbury, right down to the last leader of the opposition, never said a word against those policies. They said, let us wait until after the war to settle accounts. Now it is after the war and the same thing continues.
I said to the leader of the C.C.F. party once when he was complaining about high taxation that he had no right to complain about high taxation because he was in favour of that prodigality which has been the cause of our high taxes and strikes and troubles throughout this country. That is that. We must be realistic and keep sentiment out of trade. I said to a Tory imperialist like Mr. Hanson that we should be economically independent of Britain in regard to trade. We may be politically dependent, if the parliament of Canada desires that; but even if we are politically dependent we must be economically independent of England. That is obvious, but a dyed-in-the-wool Tory, a Tory to the core like Mr. Hanson, had nothing to say when this question was raised by myself during the war in the House of Commons. Fanaticism then ran high; the thing was forced through the house, and it is still through. I hope that the minister will be independent of England in matters of trade and that all the trade commissioners and consuls general under him will not act in virtue of instructions that come from the officials of external affairs but will act under instructions that come from himself, and that they will be independent of the English ambassador and the English high commissioner and of every British official where there is no Canadian ambassador.
[Ur. Pouliot.]
I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made enough sacrifices during the war and after the war to convince me that he wants to make a success of his job and that he wants to be just as successful as Minister of Trade and Commerce as he was as Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. I wish him good luck. I hope that he will succeed; but he will succeed only if there are no obstacles in his way, no obstacles because of undue interventions by other departments and no obstacles coming from uncalled for and untimely sentimentality which is most prejudicial to Canadian interests. It has been prejudicial to Canadian interests in the past, but I hope it will not be prejudicial any longer because the policy will have to be changed. I hope that the minister will understand that I want him to succeed by all means, so that Canada's trade will be firmly established and have a chance to develop in order that once more we may see happy days.

Surely this is old-time stuff we have been listening to, no matter how ferociously it is expressed. Surely it is nonsense today to talk about being economically independent in the matter of trade, particularly for a country like Canada. Surely it is nonsense to say that Australia and New Zealand are in competition today with Britain. Anyone who knows anything about trade knows that the trade of Australia and New Zealand is much more integrated with the trade of Britain than is Canada's trade. I venture to say that New Zealand to 75 per cent of her trade is dependent upon Britain. The people of New Zealand today are rationing themselves so that they can sell goods to Great Britain and buy goods from her. To talk today of carrying on a trade war against any country is the essence of nonsense. We cannot do that. The world is becoming aware of the fact that, instead of competitive trade, there must be co-operative trade. New Zealand and Australia are more dependent, on world trade for their prosperity than is Canada; but Canada, because of the nature of her industry and her resources is tremendously dependent on trade with other countries.
If we made loans to Britain during the war, surely Britain paid for those loans with the blood and sweat and lives of her people. We did not give anything for which we did pot get a return. As a matter of fact, Britain took the blows that would have ultimately fallen on us if she had not taken them. We ought to be proud to have been able to do our share.
There is no sloppy sentimentality in Canada's trade policies as I see them. Surely

Supply-Trade and Commerce
it is not sentiment to be realistic and to understand what must be done in the world we are living in. I am not saying this for the minister's benefit, because I am satisfied that he realizes perhaps much better than I do the necessity of co-operation in trade, and the need for building the economic resources of other countries so that they may trade with us.

I wanted to ask the
minister something about the trade with China, and I wanted to say a word on trade with Australia. I understood that our exports to China were about $30,000,000. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

speechtext: Will the minister mention two or three of the principal items? Are they lumber and cereals?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
No. The biggest item is wheat flour, $7,000,000; newsprint paper,
S4.000,000; fertilizer, $3,000,000; copper wire, $2,000,000; wheat, $2,000,000; metal-working machinery, $2,000,000; railroad ties, $1,500,000; ships, $1,500,000; machinery and parts, $1,200,000; planks, boards, et cetera, $942,000; aluminum bars, $860,000; mining machinery, $758,000; air compressors and parts, $670,000.
I understood that a substantial item was armaments. That is what I really wanted to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No, not in this list.
Is there any other list in which that would appear?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No; about $1,500,000 might be considered armaments; that is all, out of $35,000,000.
Do the preferential agreements still obtain with Australia?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes; no change.
Are sales to Australia still under the preferences which were negotiated in Ottawa in 1932?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
I understood the minister to say that there was a disturbing falling-off in some of our external markets for foreign goods. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
Would it be correct that there is no such falling-off in the natural products markets, that that is still good?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Natural products are in a worldwide short supply, so that if there is a drop in one market they are sold in another market. Necessity is driving all countries to buy raw materials to meet their requirements.

That leads me to ask this question. It seems to me that we talk a great deal about the cost of living and are all worried about it. I read a letter today which interested me, in which it was pointed out much better than I could do it, what seems to be the great trouble into which we have drifted. We have, unintentionally, of course, deprived the countryside of a great many of the people who should be raising food, and in plain words that is largely what is driving up the price of food. Are we out of balance? Have we by our policy so stimulated factory plant, and all that kind of thing, that we have drawn people by high wages into the cities and away from the business of raising food? Are we now in the position where we may find that some of these installations which we have built, no doubt in good faith, may get into trouble and not be able to manufacture their goods? On the other hand, those people who have been drawn into that kind of production might have been producing other things which we need so much at home and which we could also sell abroad. Will the minister tell me how much there is in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is a fact that we are raising far more food now than we ever did in pre-war days, and doing it with fewer men.
Not enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Our farms are being highly mechanized, and the labour requirements of producing food are not nearly as high as they were. I know of nothing that is badly out of balance so far as demand and supply of food in Canada are concerned. Our surplus of wheat is less out of proportion than it was before the war, because our population is larger and our consumption is higher. Dairy products seem to be touch and go, but I think they always were. That is about the only marginal product that I know of.

The minister has mentioned dairy products. He may tell me that he is not the Minister of Agriculture. I know that. But I have endeavoured, and without success, to learn from the Minister of Agriculture what justification there is for the policy that has shorn the hills of the eastern townships of their dairy herds. The price of feeds and butter were fixed; the margin be-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
tween the two was insufficient to enable the dairy farmer to live. If the minister can throw any light on that situation I shall be grateful to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am afraid we are out of the field and off the subject. I am not an expert on agriculture, as my hon. friend knows; I am a city man.

The minister mentioned the fact that there was a falling off in our exports of manufactured goods. Is it noticeable in any particular line? Perhaps the minister can enlarge on that a little bit. I would be interested to know in what manufactured goods there is a falling off in exports.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is a market for manufactured goods. If they fall off in one market we ship the goods to another market. Anything that Canada can manufacture today, with very few exceptions, can be sold in some market. But in speaking of a particular market such as Australia or New Zealand, there is a falling off in shipments of manufactured goods to those markets.
No over-all falling off.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No; quite the reverse.
We still have a market for everything we can manufacture?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Pretty well.

Does the minister want the committee to understand that there is a market for our manufactured goods outside the stimulated and bonused market, if I may use that phrase, to whom we have advanced credits? Are we not dependent upon those to whom we advanced credits to buy our surplus products?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Oh, no. Far and away the biggest market we have, and always has been for a great many years, is the United States. We sell in South America; we sell in the countries of Europe. A good many of them pay cash. Practically none of the credits is operative today. We are still selling our goods and expect to do so. We are an efficient country. Our goods are well priced for any market, we have been able to sell them, and we expect to continue to sell them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It seems to me that the record speaks for itself. When the war ended we lost no time in sending help to the United Kingdom and to our old customers in Europe. People talk about this stupendous help being given under the Marshall plan, ERP. Since the war, Canada has been extending relief to Europe, in proportion to our population, at more than twice the rate of the Marshall plan; well over twice. We have a record unequalled by any other country in the world. There was one purpose in it, and that was to aid in the recovery of the United Kingdom and in the recovery of our traditional customers in Europe. I am surprised that anyone would question it.

I have one. more question to ask, and it is in connection with the ban which we have placed on certain goods coming from Great Britain. I spoke about this before, and the minister said it came under the Minister of Finance. For instance, I wonder if the people of Great Britain appreciate the reason-and if there is a reason I cannot see it-for the ban being placed on any of the goods that they can manufacture and send to this country. It is all very well to talk in millions of dollars; nevertheless plenty of $5,000 items count just the same. I should like to see that ban taken off British goods coming to this country. I see that ban as something that does not help to foster good will between the two countries. I never could see any real reason why that ban should be on goods coming from any member country of the commonwealth.

What about trade between Canada and Japan? In February of this year the Vancouver Daily Province issued a leading article entitled, "Mac Arthur pledges speed-up of Canadian-Japanese trade." At that time they had apparently been in touch

Supply-Trade and Commerce
with him and he had made some statement with regard to the opening up of trade between Canada and Japan. What is the present position? _

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: All the trade with Japan is done through SCAP as they call it, or the supreme command, allied powers. It is the American military administration. We do a fair amount of business with the administration, but you can hardly call it trade with Japan. It is trade with the United States army in Japan.
Can the minister tell us what the approximate figures are?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is a small amount, covering coal, wheat and so on. We shall have the figures in a minute. It is a matter of a million or two, I think, on items such as coal and wheat.
Sales?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
Sales or purchases?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Sales.
Is the coal from Vancouver island?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is from Alberta, and perhaps from Vancouver island. It goes out through Vancouver.

The minister has said that there has been no falling off of our export of our manufactured goods; that if we cannot send them to one country, there is such a demand that we can send them to another. Do manufactured goods include processed foods? The reason I ask that question is that I understand that processors of fish are having considerable difficulty in disposing of their products.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I have referred to that matter several times. It is difficult to sell fish when every country in the world touches the ocean and catches its own fish. As they get back to normal, fish is the first item to suffer. However, fish from the maritime provinces is being sold and, as far as I know, at a good price.
I was wondering if the minister would make an exception in the case of processed fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Does my hon. friend call processed fish "manufactured goods"?
I should like to know what the minister calls it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not call it that. The hon. member can call it what he likes.

The minister says he does not call it that. That is what I want to find out. When he used the phrase "manufactured goods" he did not include processed fish. That clears that point up as far as I am concerned.
I should like to ask the minister another question and to get an answer to it, if I could.
I do not know whether I am quite in order but the question is this. I am informed that a certain make of automobile manufactured in Great Britain sells in the United States for approximately 81,300, whereas in Canada the price is approximately 81,800. What I should like to know is how this difference in price is explained? Why must we pay so much more for this car in Canada than is paid in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I am not aware of the facts.
I do not know.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall the item
carry ?
No; just a minute. I have given the minister the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Is the hon. member sure he has given me the facts?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Show us the documents. We get all kinds of these rumours.
I have given the facts as they have been given to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Yes, I know; but are they the
facts?

Does the minister say that
the facts as I have given them are not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I say that I doubt if they are correct.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Before the item is carried, as I was asked in another session to table the list of availabilities, I might make a little statement on that subject preparatory to tabling the list tomorrow.
I have already given to hon. members the general headings used in these programs, and the information has also been made available to Canadian exporters through the medium of "Foreign Trade", the official publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I have previously expressed the view that it was not desirable to publish the quantities and dollar values because of their susceptibility to misinterpretation. I must emphasize that the quantities are estimates, and estimates only, of what we believe, given certain conditions, our exporters would have available for
Supply-Trade and Commerce

shipment to Europe. The quantities, however, depend1 on many factors: for instance, the weather where agricultural produce is concerned; the availability of steel where manufactured products are concerned; and also the extent to which manufacturers may have made prior commitments. Furthermore, the statement is not exhaustive. The important recovery items have been included) in accordance with the specific request of the EGA, but information regarding a number of other commodities is being constantly made available to participating countries through our trade commissioners and to ECA officials in Washington through the Canadian embassy. With this emphasis, however, I am now prepared to table this statement which, I repeat, is not a forecast of our exports to these countries, but is an estimate of availabilities.
These estimates have not only been made available to ECA officials in Washington-
What is ECA? There are so many of these things that I have difficulty in identifying them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Economic co-operation administration. It is the Marshall plan; it is the operating part of the Marshall plan.

I was not
trying to be smart. We have so many of these things that I cannot remember them all.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I know'. I cannot remember them myself. As I say these estimates have not only been made available to ECA officials in Washington, but have also been sent to our Canadian government trade commissioners in each of the participating countries. The trade commissioners make this information available to the pertinent authorities in each of the participating countries who are responsible for drawing up their country's import requirements, and they invite these officials to indicate Canada as a preferred source of supply for those commodities which w'e know we can deliver advantageously and in competition with other countries. However, it must be realized that no one in Canada knows more about the availability of Canadian commodities than do Canadian exporters themselves; and the Department of Trade and Commerce has, therefore, repeatedly advised Canadian exporters not to depend entirely on government assistance, but rather to follow normal commercial procedures and sell their produce to European countries through their European representatives. If the commodities are such that they can be considered as recovery items, there is every likelihood that such transactions will eventually be financed by ECA dollars. It follows, therefore, that unless the Canadian

exporter is attempting to sell that type of product w'hich is recognized as a recovery item, it is not likely that he will obtain any direct ERP business. There will, howrever, be other indirect ways in which he will benefit.
I have here the printed list of Canadian commodities available to ERP countries which I will table on the orders of the day tomorrow.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I think the main commodities which were eating up our United States dollar funds were coal, oil, cotton, iron and steel; at least those are the four commodities set out in the advertisement published by the government last fall upon the announcement of the austerity program. Can the minister tell us what the position is at the present time with regard to imports of those particular commodities? Has there been any marked change in the quantities imported, or just what is the picture at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Those imports depend on the economic activity of Canada, which is high.
Upon the controls, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No. Those are necessary raw materials. For instance, we must have petroleum, and I am happy to say that the outlook for the future is greatly improved by the new discoveries in Alberta. The Leduc field may make a difference of as much as S100 million a year in United States funds by 1951, and that is encouraging.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes, and progressively up to that in the meantime. As far as coal is concerned, our properties are working to full capacity. We are exporting a certain amount of coal for United States dollars, which helps to offset imports, but our geography is such that there is a limit on the amount of coal that can be used from western Canada in central Canada, and I would say imports of coal would be about the same this year as last year.
Steel must be down.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The reason is we cannot get it. We are short of steel.
Short of dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We have the dollars to pay for it, but we cannot get the steel. It is in short supply.
What about cotton and iron?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Cotton depends on the activity in textile manufacturing, and it is about
the same as last year.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
We are bringing some from Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: These are our basic raw materials and we have to have them.
Is there any prospect of the development of iron ore in northern Quebec making a difference in importations from the United States? If so, to what extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Steep Rock has made a difference. We produced over one million tons of iron ore last year. The Sault Ste. Marie Helen mine is stepping up its output each year.
What does it produce?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Around 600,000 tons, I believe; and of course we have a great potential in northern Quebec. The trouble is that it is difficult of access. It means a large investment in railroad facilities and harbour facilities before the product can be marketed commercially.
How many years will it take?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Three or four years of development work.
Do the deposits there compare in extent with Steep Rock?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They are much greater. They have proved up over 200,000,000 tons of iron ore already, and it is known that there are over 300.000.000 tons.

Good
quality?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes, 64 per cent hematite.
Has the minister any information about falling off in shipping in and out of the port of Montreal this season, and in and out of the port of Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Our Canadian fleet is busy, but I presume my hon. friend refers not to the Canadian fleet but to all fleets. The volume of exports this year is about the same as last, and I presume shipping would be about the same.
One question about Steep Rock. Are we milling, or whatever the proper word is, that steel in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.
Are we not shipping concentrates across to the other side and buying steel back?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
That is not exactly a fair statement. Every steel company uses ore from several sources. Different ores are used
for different purposes, and all ore that is mined around the great lakes goes into what is called the great lakes ore pool. We sell the ore into the pool and it goes to dealers who handle that ore. Some comes to Canada, but the larger part goes to the United States. It is good quality ore, sold for United States dollars. We either get the ore or we get the United States dollar equivalent which we spend to buy other ore. There is no great significance in shipping Canadian ore to a Canadian steel plant when you have a situation such as exists on the great lakes.

The major portion does go south of the line in the form of ore or concentrates, or something of that kind, and we get it back here. What I have in mind is this. Where we have fuels in western Canada-I notice the Steep Rock people are draining another lake and hope to double their production within a comparatively short time-

Would the hon. member speak louder? I should like to hear what
he is saying.
I am glad you think what I am saying is worthwhile.
I always think what you say is worthwhile; you are from Alberta.

I am getting
flattery today; I got spanked the other day, I am glad to think these things alternate anyway. What I was saying was this. If we are to develop at Steep Rock, obviously they are not doing that with any small amount of ore, and is it not a possibility that, with the growth there which might easily be expected, and with fuel lying from that point not so far away, one might reasonably anticipate rather a large steel plant somewhere between those two bases of supply? That is not all imagination, is it? Is it not a possibility, the realization of which we can perhaps look forward to?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is a possibility, but my hon. friend knows that the Mesabi ore deposits back of the Duluth area have been coming through in great volume, and there is no steel plant near Mesabi, or near Duluth.
It is running out.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Y'es, and we hope that Steep Rock is helping to take its place. I do not know that it follows, because you have ore in the country, that you must necessarily have steel in the country. If you had a combination of ore and coal in the same locality,
Supply-Trade and Commerce

undoubtedly you would have steel manufacture, but it is difficult to imagine either hauling coal from Alberta to the head of the lakes or hauling ore from Steep Rock to Alberta or some intermediate point.

When the import-export act was passed we had a statement from some of the staff, indicating the basis on -which export permits were granted and the extent to which the ordinary conduct of business was being supervised by the officials. I wish the minister would say a word or two on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There are two bases for controls; one is the basis of shortage. There are certain commodities we must keep in the country to an extent sufficient to keep our own economy going.
Notably?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Steel is an excellent example. When it comes to permitting the export of steel in the form of manufactured goods we tend to give a preference to the most highly manufactured, for instance, steel for at least
11,000	a ton. Therefore we permit the export of steel in the form of locomotives and in various other forms-
Machinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Machine tools, and agricultural machinery, which is a sort of border-line case. We do not get very much for steel per ton in agricultural implements, but they are badly needed abroad and we allow them to be exported. That, however, is the criterion. If someone wants to export tin cans we are not allowing them to do so. We do not allow manufactures which mean very little other than rolling plate into some form and sending it out.
Rails?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
No; nails are absolutely
barred.
I said rails.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
We have rail capacity. It is a finished product made both at Sydney and at Sault Ste. Marie. It is one of the few products they can make; and therefore we allow them to manufacture into rails steel not required for other purposes. If there is an excess
fMr. Howe.]
beyond the requirements of our own railways we allow it to be exported. There is very little exported, though. Most of the rails manufactured at both places are used in Canada.
I take it that the fact that there is a decrease in the item indicates that the business of controlling exports is not growing too fast. May I take it that perhaps it is actually lessening.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We have taken a good many items off control, as they have moved into adequate supply. At the end of December we had 520 articles under control, and at June 15 we had only 466. The list is going down.

Is fish on the export list? An article appeared in the Montreal Star, which stated that dealers in Puerto Rico or Costa Rica-I am not sure which it was, but it was one of those Central American countries -were complaining about the Canadian fish going to their country. It was coming in short supply, and they felt that this was because the people bringing it in wanted to keep the price up.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is not and never has been any export control on fish.
I suggest that the minister's department should check that complaint.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I shall do so.
In view of the fact that several large pulp operators in Ontario are exporting raw pulp, is it necessary for them to get permits to do so from either the dominion or provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Pulpwood, yes; manufactured wood pulp, no.
Does the minister not think it would be more beneficial if that pulpwood were made into paper here, instead of the raw material being shipped?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
Will the government take steps to see if it can be done?
The Ontario government is doing it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It means building more paper mills. They are being built right along.
What is the situation with regard to the export of wheat, oats, barley and buckwheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
All wheat is exported and sold abroad through the Canadian wheat board. This being a year of a short crop, it is chiefly being delivered to the United Kingdom to fill

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
an existing contract. Any wheat we have surplus to that is being sold in other traditional markets. Our difficulty is not to sell wheat; it is to find enough wheat to fill our obligations.
We had a short crop of coarse grains, and it was estimated that our supplies of oats and barley would not be more than enough to meet domestic requirements. We find at the end of the year that we have a small surplus of about ten million bushels of oats and about the same amount of barley, which at the present time is being sold in the world market at the best prices obtainable.
We have allowed rye to move freely. It is not a food grain in Canada.
It is a beverage grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Well, not much of that, either.
No whisky is made out of rye now. Do not let us get this mixed up.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Rye has nothing to do with rye whisky, I know.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Flax seed has been under control, and under the international allocation. We dispose of our flax seed as directed by the international food organization. Just now we have a small surplus and are selling it freely in the rvorld market.
What about buckwheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Buckwheat is not an export commodity. It is fed to hens.
Is 'the department still charging for the permit in connection with coarse grains the difference between the Canadian and export prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Where there is a pool, as there is in wheat, oats and barley, an equalization fee is charged where grain is sold to other than contract countries. For example, if a man wishes to sell oats in the United States he is charged1 the difference between the domestic price and the export price and pays an equalization fee. The money so recovered is put into the oats pool.
Is he charged for his permit?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: He is charged the equalization fee.
Out of the amount of this item I see that $98,400 is for temporary assistance. Would the minister explain why the expenditure for temporary assistance is about 99 per cent of the total vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The branch is a temporary one. We hope that export controls are a passing phase of the Canadian economy. Therefore we cannot put on too many permanent employees to administer a temporary job.
How much oats and barley went to the United States from this country last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am sorry I have not that figure, but I shall be glad to make an announcement on the point when the orders of the day are called.
