I should think the coal problem comes under the departmental administration item?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is item 396.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Under the rule we have followed, the hon. member may discuss anything he likes under the departmental administration item.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak about coal. From about the middle of March to the end of the month people in Ontario who were users of coal were still in a daze over the trouble they had to obtain it during the winter. I was one of those people. The problem of coal had a great deal to do with the recent provincial election. People w'ere still exasperated over their inability to get coal, and from reading in the daily papers that they had better place their orders immediately for next winter's supply.
Quite a number of people in Ontario-I have forgotten exactly how many-got together and consulted with some gentlemen in Toronto about holding a dinner meeting here in Ottawa so as to bring before the authorities the absolute necessity for Canada to make every possible effort to produce coal in this country, particularly for use in the two central provinces. The other provinces either have coal or are close to a supply of it.
On April 28, as a result of the organization of coal users, a big dinner was held at the Chateau Laurier hotel in Ottawa. I have forgotten whether the chairman was there-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I was not there.

I know the minister was not; lie sent me a note saying he could not attend. However, his parliamentary assistant was there. That evening 206 distinguished men from all parts of Canada, and two ladies,
How much would that cost?

About 11,500,000 or $2,000,000. That does not mean anything when one considers what could be brought out and what it would save in United States dollars. At the present time we are importing $150 million worth of United States coal. We bring in four to five million tons of anthracite coal from the United States, mostly to the Ontario market. For that we pay $150 million in United States funds, plus the freight charges to bring it to the border, which totals another $75 million. There is a grand total of approximately $225 million in real United States coin that is paid out every year.
We would not be able to save all of that in a year or two, but the sooner we start to try to save it, the better it will be for our dollar situation. Even if Sir Albert Braithwaite could produce only two million tons of hard coal next year, it would mean a great deal. Some people in the department try to tell me it is not ham coal. I have read a report from the department, a report I do not like at all. It does not strike me as an honest effort-I do not mean it is dishonest-to produce Canadian coal for the Ontario market. If we can buy four million tons a year of hard coal from Alberta, what a tremendous business that would mean back and forth between Alberta, Ontario and Quebec, and think what it would mean in Canadian employment and in Canadian freight. The Canadian railroads now get only $5 a ton for hauling United States coal from the border.
How does the coal compare in B.T.U.?
One hundred per cent. I have seen engineers' analyses, and they show that the coal is very high in B.T.U. and very low in ash, a good coal from every point of view.
And low in moisture.

And low in moisture. I am hoping that the hon. member for Calgary West, who must know Alberta coal much better than I do, will support what I say in this regard. It is a No. 1 coal and would save the situation in the central provinces, and save also many millions of United States dollars.
The last clause of this report says:
The commission is convinced that if these ventures-
That is these two big mining areas in the Alberta foothills.
-result in the opening of new mines, the coals produced will exhibit marked friability, thus presenting serious marketing problems.
I do not think the man who wrote that knows the first thing about it. He was not talking about the coal I am talking about. I take the statement of those who have had to do with it. I take the statement of Sir Albert Braithwaite, who has no axe to grind except to help Canada produce coal. There is a lot behind this story, if it all came out, and it would be a sorry story if all I have heard is true.
At that same meeting a capable minister of this government, the Minister of Agriculture, made an outstanding address. I never heard a better one. I told him afterwards, "If you make an address like that you will sweep the Liberal convention." I am taking no sides in that, of course, but I do like to hear a man talk who knows what he is talking about, and he certainly knew what he was talking about that night. I am going to read what he said. I do not want any minister to think I am boosting the Minister of Agriculture; I am not boosting anybody; but I was overjoyed with his address, as the whole audience was. This is what he said.
I am not going to tell you how little was left of the money at the time that I took it over.
He was speaking of the money that was left when he was made minister of labour and resources in a former Saskatchewan government. He had used some money for the development of coal at Estevan, which was later shipped to Manitoba. It changed over the whole process of coal production in the west by substituting Canadian coal for Manitoba, for coal that formerly came from the United States. He went on:
We know a great deal of him-
He was speaking of Mr. Mervyn Brown.
-in the province of Saskatchewan as a promoter of the welfare of industrial development in the western part of Canada.
The Minister of Agriculture came out strongly in favour of developing these hard coals in the Highwood area for shipment to the central provinces. Like everybody else present, I was delighted with what the Minister of Agriculture said, because that is the program I had been advocating for years and years, to develop our own coal resources in Canada and exchange trade back and forth between our own provinces.

Does the long haul cause any trouble?

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

No. The coal produced by strip-mining, including the haul, would sell in Ontario at $14 a ton, thereby saving the Ontario coal user no less than $5 a ton, which would amount to $40 to $50 during the winter, to the average householder.
Is it all rail, or rail and lake?

All rail. When the coal is loaded on the train it comes through just as cheaply one way as the other.
I received a telegram from Mr. Greenfield, the day of the dinner, a former premier of Alberta, regretting that he could not attend the meeting. I should like to read it:
Regret previous engagements prevent acceptance your kind invitation to dinner Chateau Laurier April 28. Alberta possesses undeveloped hard coal in abundance proven by analysis and by tests in Ontario household equipment to be of a quality that can successfully compete with American anthracite in Ontario markets and stand up to outdoor storage without deterioration.
You do not need anything better than that.
I trust that the important gathering on the 28th will convince those present of the urgent necessity of developing Canadian coal resources both hard and steam coal for the benefit of Canadian citizens east and west and in so doing make a substantial and helpful contribution towards easing Canada's pressing dollar problem. The time for action is now-not years hence.
I take the same stand. An investment $1,500,000 to bring out millions of tons of coal from Alberta mines to save United States dollars would be a tremendous worthwhile investment for us, besides saving the coal user in the central provinces $5 a ton.
Reference was made to what happened between 1920 and 1925 when a policy of using coal from Alberta revolutionized coal usage in. Manitoba and meant a changeover from ninety per cent of the United States coal that had formerly been imported, to Canadian coal. We can do the very same thing now if we only wake up and develop our own resources. If I were sitting in the minister's chair I would not pay a particle of attention to his coal board, if they say Alberta cannot do it; I would be all the more inclined to tell them to pick up their hats and move on. We want Alberta hard coal and we shall be glad to get Nova Scotia soft coal. By using Alberta coal, the coal user in the central provinces would save $5 a ton; the country would save millions in United States dollars, and freight would go to our own Canadian railways. In a few days time we shall have an estimate before us to make good a deficit of $85,000,000 on the Canadian railfMr. Hackett,]
ways. I am for giving that to them, but the speediest way of getting rid of those deficits is to bring more freight to our railways. One way is by letting them haul hard coal from Alberta to the central provinces, and then they will not need to come to parliament so often for fifty, sixty or seventy-five million dollars.
I know that others would like to speak on this question, and I should like to hear from the hon. member for Calgary West, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the hon. member for Lethbridge and others. Mr. Chairman, the time has come for action. Canadians must wake up. The money we paid in United States dollars for coal and freight on it from the United States amounts to $225 million a year. That would be one of the soundest ways for the minister to overcome his difficulties. If he gets my conception of this I know he will put his teeth into it and do the job. That is one sound way to save United States dollars, and to save Ontario coal users $5 a ton. One company-there are two of them-guarantees to deliver hard coal at not more than $14 a ton to Ontario users. This coal looks to me to be as good as United States anthracite. It is just as good in every way. It looks to me to be sound business to do that. Besides that it will give Canadian workmen employment.
I was sorry the minister was not there that night. His parliamentary assistant was there, and I am sure that he was impressed by Sir Albert Braithwaite and his statement. If we give him a chance by investing just $1,500,000, and build a short spur line not more than fifty miles long, he will at once invest $1,000,000, and the company would invest $1,000,000, to bring in a million dollars worth of machinery and build tipples, et cetera. That looks to me like sound business. I cannot understand why in the intervening two months the parliamentary assistant has not encouraged the minister, the coal board and the railways to get busy and do something for Canada, so that they will not be coming to this parliament over and over again for more and more money, but will be hauling freight produced in Canada, and spending the money in Canada.
I do not intend to go any farther, because I want others to say something on this. With all the strength I have, I plead with the minister to adopt a Canadian coal policy, of which one program would be moving hard coal from Alberta to Ontario, as well as Drum-heller coal. I use it myself sometimes. I understand that all the Drumheller coal that can be produced can be sold in Alberta and the west and that the companies undertake

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
not to try to sell any hard coal in the west but to send it to the east. There should also be a program of moving Nova Seotia coal to the central provinces. Let us have a national coal policy now-the sooner the better.

I started to speak on another subject on the Department of Trade and Commerce administration item. While I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Davenport, and agreed with everything he said on the subject of coal, I am going to reserve my remarks on that subject until we come to the item which has to do with the operation of the dominion coal board. I think my remarks on that subject would be more appropriate there.
The remarks I have to make tonight deal with a general situation that I think is not covered by any particular item, but definitely comes within the scope of the minister's activities. The reason I am going to make a short statement tonight is that I believe the recent increase permitted in steel calls for a statement and explanation by the minister.
In the light of present inflationary prices in Canada, I cannot understand how the minister or the government can justify permitting another price increase in one of our basic commodities that is going to have a terrific effect on the whole price structure in Canada. I do not think it was justified, according to the figures that I have seen. I do not think it was fair to the workers employed in steel plants who entered into agreements with their employers in 1946, a two-year agreement, and a slight adjustment in wages in 1948, which was done with the view of stabilizing the industry, trying to increase production, lower costs and in general stabilize that basic industry. This increase in steel permitted to the steel companies of Canada, without any consultation with the steel workers' union, was a breach of good faith. It definitely brings into focus what was proposed by the steel union workers when we met with them in the industrial relations committee early in 1946. At that time they proposed that a joint council for the industry should be established consisting of representatives of the union, of the industry and of the government, so that they might from time to time sit in and consider the kind of matter about which I am now speaking, namely, a general increase in the price of basic steel.
That was not done. They were not consulted. I consider it was a breach of good faith on the part of the government in at least not letting them know, in view of the reasonable stand they took in 1948 with regard to the adjustment of their wages.
It is unfortunate that we have to pick up our information in the press in matters of this
kind. Announcements like these should be made in the house rather than through the medium of the press. I picked it up in a press report. I am going to place a few figures on record to bear out what I am saying. I do not think the minister can justify the increase at this time, on the basis of profits or production, to say nothing of the upward trend in prices generally in Canada. The price increase permitted is practically the same as was permitted in 1945. We know when that first steel increase was granted in 1945. In my opinion that was the increase which wrecked the whole price structure. That is my honest opinion. If steel had been held at that time, and controls had been maintained for another couple of years at least, we would not have got away to the inflationary spiral we are now in.
On rods there is an increase of $5 a ton permitted; plate, $12 a ton; bars, $5 a ton; sheets, $7 a ton; skelp, $12 a ton, or an average increase of $8.20 a ton on all steel, both raw and processed. I do not think the increase can be justified for this reason. Three of the large steel producers in Canada are Algoma, Dosco and Stelco. Their profits in 1946 were $4,306,928. In 1947 they were $8,608,447, a terrific increase. The total tonnage in 1947 was 2,155,261.
According to the Financial Post which is out ahead of time-I notice that the paper I have here is dated June 19, which is Saturday-the Dosco company at Sydney have broken all records in steel production. If that is true, it should lower costs and should eliminate the necessity for an increase in the price of steel. There is quite a story in the Financial Post, but I do not want to take the time of the committee in telling it. On the basis of the average increase of $8.20 a ton, the profits of the three companies in 1948, based on the production I have just mentioned, should be approximately $17,673,140.20, or an increase of approximately $9,000,000 in profits to the three operating companies.
How does the government justify its action in permitting the increase at this time? According to the press report that I have here, the government justifies the increase on the ground that it was removing the $2,500,000 subsidy that it was paying on steel. In the face of the huge surplus, the government had in the last budget, it saved the $2,500,000 subsidy that it was paying on steel. The government grants a price increase that will cost money to the consumers in Canada, because in the final analysis it is the consuming public that will have to pay it. The government throws back the load of subsidizing these companies-and it is a subsidy-to increase their profits by approximately $9,000,000, in order to save $2,500,000 by way of subsidy. It does not

Su-p-ply-Reconstruction and Supply
add up. The reason I am making the statement now is that I want the minister to make to this committee some statement as to why this increase is permitted at this time.
The timing is terrible right now when everyone you meet in this country is talking about the price of beef and the price of butter, with prices jumping five to six cents in a day on a pound of butter. When that kind of thing is going on, the minister must have some idea of the mental attitude of the people toward this kind of thing. What I am fearful of is this. I know how difficult it was in 1945 to get a settlement with workers in the industry; and then, being closely in touch with them because that large steel plant in Sydney is in my riding, I know how reasonable and fair those boys were in 1948 in adjusting their wages. The one thing they did not want was any disturbance in the industry. Their minds were made up that they would increase production, try to lower costs, and try to get some stability in the industry after the transfer from war to peace. I know that from going through the shops. I have letters from them in which they say, "Not consulted"; "We know nothing about it"; "This thing is thrown at us through the press. Try to get some information from the minister." They did not think this action can be justified.
I do not intend to say anything more about the matter. I have made my statement. I have set out figures there that I want the minister to try to clarify for the benefit of the general public in Canada. If that process is continued until that increase gets into farm machinery, enters into the cost of the things the farmer produces, and then is reflected in the general cost of living across Canada, it will be the thing that will break the camel's back. The people will revolt against that kind of thing. In my opinion that increase is not justified. The extra profits given these companies by reason of this increase cannot be justified. The removal of that $2,500,000 subsidy and the passing of it back to the consumers of Canada is something the minister must explain. I should like to have it explained.

Mr. Chairman-

I want to speak about Alberta coal, but before doing so I cannot avoid making a remark or two in reply to at least a few of the things that were said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and to one of them in particular. I have heard all my life about that last straw that breaks the camel's back. I should like to recall to him something that happened in his own union in Nova Scotia. An increase in wages was granted there, on the basis that the employees in those mines should increase their per ton per man production in that mine; and they did, may I say, increase it. But there are other things that may break the camel's back. One of them is this. Any industry which is unable to produce per man a certain volume, just cannot live. In that case-the one I referred to in his own union-that was proved conclusively.
Do you want me to explain how that was done.
Would you mind letting me have a little go? Then you can take all the time you want to explain.
I want to clarify it.
It was because of your men working harder and using their machinery better.
No, it was not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Calgary West has the floor.
I am telling the hon. member he is absolutely incorrect; and if he does not want the matter clarified that is up to him. I can tell him how it was done.
You can give me theories, and no one can equal you in this House of Commons in theorizing.
It is not theory.
A moment ago the hon. member said, Mr. Chairman, that an increase in wages did not increase costs.
I did not.
Well, I am sorry if I misunderstood.
I said it could be offset.
The hon. member said it did not necessarily increase costs. But it does.
That is where lawyers are at fault. They do not know economics.

What I have said applies to every intake product in your operation, whether it foe labour, goods or anjdhing else. Simple arithmetic is still good, and that indicates that if your cost increases for the things you buy, then, of course, it increases the cost of your product. Never until tonight have I heard that principle departed from anywhere; and I had to come to this House of Commons, this place of such a high level of intelligence, to hear that principle disputed tonight.
With respect to our coal position, I am not unmindful of the fact that the hon. member for Davenport had an excellent dinner, and I am not disputing the fact that there is a problem to be solved in this coal business in my own province. I wonder if I might take a moment of the time of the committee to explain geographically what the whole situation is out there. On the prairies, practically wherever you drill holes in the ground, you will find lignite coal, which is a soft coal containing plenty of moisture, and of course when you ship that coal you ship moisture. It is rather hard to pay freight on moisture when it does not help to heat your house or anything of that kind. But going back into the mountains, on the eastern slopes of the rockies, you begin at the south and fortunately it does not extend beyond the United

States border. I am not being unkind to the Americans, but fortunately for our economy it does not.
If you go along the Crowsnest pass a matter of twenty miles or so, you will find coal seams exposed through there, all of which are being worked at the present time, and that is what is know as bituminous coal. In other words, it is industrial coal used in our engines. Then you follow that line north, and the next place which is worked in quantities is at Nordegg, which is west of Red Deer. You go farther, following the same line pretty much, until you come to excellent bituminous mines in what we call the coal branch, which is the branch running out of Edson, south of Edson, Edson being roughly 150 to 160 miles from Edmonton.
There we have good bituminous coal. Of late years, particularly in the northern area, strip-mining has become something of real value. You see, Mr. Chairman, it is all right to talk about strip-mining at Estevan, Saskatchewan, because the over-burden is soil or clay or something of that kind. The operation is a simple one. You do not need to be a miner. You go out with a big scoop, and you throw the stuff to one side and scoop the coal out with the same kind of machinery and throw it into boxcars and ship it. Then you fill the trench you have made, and on and on you go. They have an over-burden that is rather heavy but easily got up. These better quality mines in the mountains have an overburden that is mostly rock, which is difficult and much more costly to remove.
And so, up in that northern area, we have some strip-mining, but on account of physical conditions it does not amount to a great deal. At Cadomin they have new strip-mining and at present they produce five tons to one with deep-mining or shaft-mining. Anyone therefore can readily see that that operation is a comparatively cheap one.
That coal varies greatly in that sweep from south to north. Some of it will coke. They are coking, and they are using it at the International at Coleman and a good deal at Michel, the Crowsnest Pass Coal Company property some miles further away. Then you come to Nordegg, immediately west of Red Deer, midway between Calgary and Edmonton, about 100 or 200 miles. It is right in the middle. There you have good coal, but it is so fine that they have had to put in a briquetting plant, and briquettes are produced because they mix with this very fine coal in order to have it made useful in the running of locomotives. The product is almost completely sold to the railways.

At this place, on these rivers which are southwest of Calgary, and of which the hon. member for Davenport was speaking, there are two rivers coming out; one is the Sheep river and the other the Highwood river. They rise in the Highwood range close together and then spread, one going through Turner valley; and the Highwood, which is farther south, goes through High River, the Sheep into Highwood, and the Highwood into Bow, and that ends the confluence of the waters there. The mine which the hon. member for Davenport spoke about is on the Sheep river which is directly west of Turner valley.
The other property or mine, if you like, is on the Highwood river, and I would think the distance between the Sheep river mine, which we know as the Burns mine, and the other on the Highwood river, which we know as the Ford mine, is about twenty to twenty-five miles. I am guessing, but I would think there is continuous coal between these two mines.
When I speak of continuous coal, I have no personal knowledge of the mine which has been discussed tonight. All I know is hearsay. But this other property on the Highwood I have visited. I have been there and stayed for days, and there are five seams on that property which I have seen, varying from five feet, which is the narrowest strip, to forty feet in width. I do not know how high this chamber is; probably it is twice that height, or something like that. Conceive, Mr. Chairman, a seam of coal half the height of this chamber. I have seen them mining some rather thick seams, and the only way they can do so is by building benches in it. In that way they take down the coal.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Davenport say-at least I got the impression from what he said-that this coal may be mined in lumps. That may be so, but one thing I know about the Highwood end' of the picture, that is the Ford property, is that it is coal which is very friable. It breaks up into fine particles when it is mined. We also know that in your market here in the eastern provinces, in Ontario and Quebec, you have been used all your lives to dealing with Pennsylvania coal which used to come in pieces which were about half the size of an egg and were bright and shiny black coal. That was years ago. Even from observation of coal ears as I ride in the trains, I know you are not getting that now or anything like it. You are not getting the Pennsylvania coal you got here some years ago.
I think I should say I know something about the heating quality of this coal on the Highwood. I was there with the chief engineer

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
and he asked me to watch him and time him. In the cabin we had a round little stove. It was not a Quebec heater but an ordinary little stove made of tin, I thought, or thin iron. At night he put in the stove a shovelful of what appeared to me, used as I was to Drum-heller coal, to be lignite, which is mined in big shiny pieces as big as you want. He put that in at eleven o'clock at night. I never was a very early riser, and I was not then. But at ten o'clock in the morning there was the grandest little cone of very hot fuel under the ashes in that stove that one could ever see. So let no one have any doubt about the heating qualities of that coal, or about its ability to maintain a fire overnight.
I now come to something of which I am not sure. We hear of lignite, bituminous, subbituminous and anthracite coal. I know all about B.T.U.'s. One B.T.U. is the heat required to raise a pound of water one degree, if my memory serves me correctly. But to most people the difficulty is this. Is that coal an anthracite? The division is an artificial one. I am not sure about this; but I do not think we have any generalized term, such an anthracite, which would apply to a given coal. In other words, if your volatility, your lack of moisture, your lack of ash or your British thermal units-B.T.U.'s-are of a certain quality, it means that this coal is just as good as the coal over there which it is said has those various qualities within the coal itself.
A coal commission sat for some considerable time. Two of the members came from my own province. They were, and are, close personal friends. The man Brown, to whom the hon. member for Davenport referred, appeared before the hearing. It is part of the record of that commission that the solicitor for Mr. Brown wrote to the commission saying he would not appear further before them on account of his objection to two of the members at the commission-those two being my two personal friends I mentioned a while ago.
I am sorry that- attitude was taken. I am not giving an ex post facto judgment. I am not saying anyone was right or anyone was wrong; but I do know that this coal which the hon. member for Davenport has introduced into the discussion tonight is not thoroughly considered in that report. Let me say in passing that I am not placing fault or blame anywhere. Certainly I am not in any position to do that. But at one time my office acted for this Highwood end of the picture, which was supported largely by a man from New York, one from Cincinnati and one from Montreal. I may say it is years since my office has been solicitor for this concern.

It is now largely in the hands of Mr. Sweezey of Montreal, and they are trying to build their own railway.
But what I am saying is this, that from the observations of an amateur like myself, I have no doubt whatever as to the heat there is in this coal. I have no doubt whatever as to its ability to maintain a fire for a long time. That, of course, is not true of our lignite coal. I also have no doubt whatever as to its ability to be stored for some considerable time because, as I say, it is almost completely lacking in moisture.
Many of us have travelled up and down our railways in years gone by, and we have seen immense piles of coal stored along the rights of way of both the railway companies. It is true that- occasionally we have seen some smoke rising, and we know there was fire down there. But the railway people will tell you that that loss is practically nothing; it is only one in ten or twenty piles that ignites at all. The loss is nothing because, as the minister well knows, coal burning without oxygen, or practically without oxygen, makes very little progress.
We have mines afire out there in the bitu

minous field. For example, the first Cadomin mine has been afire for many years. True, they abandoned it; and yet the progress of that fire has been practically nothing. It is a very, very slow process. That is the mine- and let me say, it was a wonderful mine- which was on the top slope with the railway right below. They never had a tipple; all they had was a coal chute. They mined it and took it down onto the cars. Then the thing caught fire. What did they do? They went up top, took two creeks and diverted them into the mine, closed it up at the bottom and shut the works off for a month. When they were through, the fire was still going, so they abandoned it and went across that great ravine the minister knows is there to do their mining on the other side.
What is all this about? I am not going to repeat what was said by the hon. member for Davenport, except to agree with him most heartily 'that this coal program, particularly for people in eastern Canada, is one of the most serious problems with which you are faced. I can remember the minister telling us, either last year or the year before, when we had some difficulty with shipping, that he was trying to get cars to bring it around the end, or through the middle, to avoid water transportation, to keep this province of Ontario from being cold,, or even from freezing.
So I repeat what I said before, that to me this matter is one of grave concern to the dominion. We should not be dependent upon.

There is another fallacy in discussing this matter, and that is talking about coal in Alberta as being analogous to coal in Toronto. The two have no relation. In the war we had a serious shortage of domestic coal in Toronto, and I went out, regardless of expense, to bring western coal to Toronto. I think I used every transportation facility that was

available, and the best I could do was to bring about half a million tons of Alberta coal to Toronto a year. We have never moved as much as one million tons of Alberta coal into Toronto in a year, and unless the railway facilities are tremendously increased we never can. Coal is bulky and a carload of coal does not contain many tons. The number of carloads involved in moving a million tons of coal presents a serious transportation problem.
I wish we could get enough Alberta coal to fill the requirements of the prairie provinces. Today the Alberta mines are working to capacity twelve months in the year, and still we have to move United States coal back as far as Saskatoon.
There is an answer to that. Alberta coal during the war has gone west. Before the war we moved it into two divisions beyond Kenora.

I know it was able to fill that market, but with the great step-up there has been in industry, all the coal the mines are producing is being used and we are still moving United States coal into Saskatoon. Let us take care of the western problem before we get down to Toronto.
The government has a policy of subventions; that policy is sufficiently elastic and will be administered so that all the coal that Canada [DOT]can produce both east and west will be moved *to Canadian markets, and we will move it as far as is necessary. It is not a question of this particular mine being related to some particular market. We can find a market without any difficulty whatever for all the coal we can produce.
The only difficulty with Brown and his associates is that they want someone else to furnish the money to develop a mine. They had the idea and they want someone else to furnish the money. That is laudable, but the problem is 'theirs, not the government's. I want a little information from the minister with regard to contracts which have yet to be liquidated. I should like to know what were the principal amounts paid and how far the contracts have been liquidated.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I was going to make a statement on the work of the department; and since this is a disappearing department. I think I should do so. I have a preamble dealing with the greatness of the department which perhaps I can omit. This shows the present position pretty well.
The Department of Reconstruction and Supply resulted from the amalgamation at the end of 1945 of the wartime Department of Munitions and Supply, and the Department of Reconstruction, established in June, 1944. The department was considered necessary to discharge certain temporary functions in connection with the liquidation of Canada's war effort and the re-establishment of Canadian industry on a peacetime footing.
The department has been in process of dissolution from the time of its establishment. ^ The department's staff and functions have continued to contract during the past year. In some cases this has taken place because work has been wound up. In other cases functions of a more continuing nature have been transferred or are in the process of transfer to other departments.
The liquidation of the war program involved four responsibilities: (1) the termination and settlement of war contracts and the renegotiation of war contracts where participating firms had realized large profits; (2) the liquidation of surplus war plant and other forms of war equipment; (3) the dissolution or other disposition of crown companies established during the war, and (4) the disposition of controls in existence at the end of the war.
This is what my hon. friend was asking for. On the first point, as indicated before, war contract cancellations, in the closing phases of the war and immediately thereafter, involved $2,500 million. In many instances these cancellations have not involved any claims, but where claims were made they were dealt with by the contracts settlement board of the department. This board has now approved claims for the settlement of these contracts for about $290 million, which represents about 96 per cent of all the claims submitted. In other words, we have about four per cent of the claims still to be settled.
The department has also been engaged in the renegotiation of contracts made during the war. The result of these efforts was to reduce war contracts by over $475 million, of which all but $80,000,000 have been fully settled.
On the second point, the liquidation of surplus war plant and other equipment has been in the hands of War Assets Corporation. This corporation has now disposed of most of the war surplus in the hands of the Dominion of Canada. Sales of war surpluses brought $430 million to the treasury by the end of May, 1948. However, it will still take some more time to clean up the tag ends of disposal work.
On the third point, the disposition of crown companies established during the war has been completed by now. Of the thirty crown companies operating under the Department of Munitions and Supply at the conclusion of the war, twenty-six have now been liquidated. The four which continue to function on a peacetime basis in the same or altered form are:	Canadian Arsenals Limited; Polymer
Corporation Limited; Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited; and Wartime Housing Limited, which has now been absorbed by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. These companies have hitherto been reporting to parliament through the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. Since this portfolio is a temporary one while the crown companies have continuing functions to perform, arrangements are being made to have these crown companies report to parliament through the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Similarly, the dominion coal board,

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
established last year, will henceforth be reporting to parliament through the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
On the fourth point, we have abolished all controls formerly exercised by the Department of Munitions and Supply and its successor, the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, except for allocation controls over steel, timber and building materials and the use of priorities to assure an adequate supply of building materials to priority projects. The administrators of the controls are finding it possible, by negotiating with the interested parties, to obtain the desired allocation of materials on a voluntary basis. These informal arrangements work very well and are much more desirable from the point of view of both the government and industiy, and give a flexibility that could not otherwise be obtained. These allocation controls are continuing on a temporary basis, and we hope to dispose of them as soon as economic conditions warrant it. We are hopeful that this will be possible at the time when the Department of Reconstruction and Supply is folded up.
In connection with the administration of the foreign exchange regulations brought into force on November 17, 1947, an emergency import control branch was set up in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply to control the import of capital goods. Personnel for this division have been recruited within the department, and in the Department of Trade and Commerce. Under the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act, provision was made for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to administer import controls over capital goods. This is an advantageous arrangement, because it permits the co-ordination of import controls with the work done by various commodity officers in the Department of Trade and Commerce. Therefore, as soon as administrative details can be dealt with, the personnel of the emergency import control branch, now with the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, will be transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The rest of the statement refers to other continuing functions which can be dealt with as we proceed with the estimates.

This is a brief statement from the settlement officer of the contracts settlement board.
The following is a brief summary of the operations of the contract settlement board up to May 31, 1948, which may be treated as supplementary to the report dated May 29, 1947, submitted by the secretary of the board.
The board received a total of 3,252 termination notices up to 31st March, 1947. All contracts current at that date were taken over by Canadian Commercial Corporation.
The board has received a total of 3,707 claims, of -which 455 were cancelled or withdrawn, leaving a balance of 3,252 claims amounting to $301,183,453 to be dealt with.
A total of 3,251 claims amounting to $289,142,367 have been approved, or 96 per cent of amount claimed. The value of the uncompleted portion of the terminated contracts was $2,479,339,070, and the total of claims approved represents 11-6 per cent of this amount.
One claim for approximately $2,037,411 is awaiting final review. The production under this contract for maintenance kits for wireless sets was only recently completed. Included in the amount approved are seven claims by one contractor totalling $1,148,397, which are being amended as result of further audit investigation. There is also one claim outstanding awaiting further audit investigation which may take some time.
Payments have been made to contractors in accordance with amount approved, and the contingent liability due to revision in the claims is comparatively small and should not exceed $150,000 in all.
